articles.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
articles.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV had only recently returned from a trip to France when he announced doctors had found a nodule on his lungImage: Grzegorz Galazka/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.
At under 3 cm (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.
In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.
What we know so far
All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."
That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.
Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

At the same time, the risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules." That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.
Fortunately, however, many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.
It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.
What are lung nodules?
Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.
Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.
Causes and symptoms of lung nodules
Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.
At more than 3 cm, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.
What makes lung nodules cancerous?
It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.
At 2 mm or smaller the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 mm.
The risk of cancer becomes 9-10% at about 8 to 10 mm. And at larger than 1 cm, the risk of cancer is about 15%.
The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.
There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.
According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."
A journey through lung health
Lung nodules and lung cancer are common
It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."
However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

articles.title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
articles.summary: Shadrack Sibiya had denied grooming a 16-year-old and raping an 18-year-old.

blocks.text: South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking.
Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied.
Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.

The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

In a "24 Oras" report by Jonathan Andal, the word buwaon means “sinungaling (liar)” in Waray.
“Ay bakit mo sinabi (why did you tell them)… That’s just supposed to be [between] the two of us,” Marcos asked Castro during his Kapihan with the media in Singapore on Sunday.

Castro first shared the word with the media when asked about Marcos’ reaction to Vice President Sara Duterte’s allegations that his administration was desperate to bring her down and was pushing for Charter Change to stop the 2028 national elections.
“Ito po ang mismong mensahe ng Pangulo: Mga buwaon. Translate natin, mga sinungaling,” Castro said during a palace briefing on September 28.
(This is the message of the President: Mga buwaon. Let's translate, liars.)
During the Kapihan, Marcos explained that he uttered the word during a conversation with Castro, whom he had asked to verify reports regarding Duterte’s allegations against the administration.

“I just got this report, and I asked [her], ‘Is it true that this report came out?’ And ‘yon ang comment ko sa kaniya. Akala niya press release na pala ‘yon. ‘Kaw talaga. Ante Kler talaga oh,” the President said.
(I just received the report and asked her, ‘Is it true that this report came out?’ That was simply my comment to her. She thought it was already an official press release. Oh, Usec. Claire.)
Castro humorously offered an apology, to which Marcos playfully responded that they would discuss the matter further in private.
Marcos emphasized that Duterte’s allegations were indeed “fake news.” He challenged the Vice President to prove her claims and present evidence.
“Well, this is fake news. Prove it. You’re saying that based on what?” the President said.
Super El Niño
In preparation for Super El Niño, Marcos advised the public to start harvesting rainwater to ensure they do not run out of supply.
“Bumili na kayo ng balde, para 'pag umulan, makolekta na ninyo lahat,” Marcos said.
(Buy water containers ahead, so that when it rains you can collect all of it.)
He added that the government will distribute water filters and teach citizens how to safely treat rainwater for consumption.
“We’ll give you a filter, we’ll teach you how to do everything para hindi kayo magkasakit at maayos ang pag-treat ng tubig, pag-filter ng tubig,” the President said.
(We’ll give you a filter and teach you how to do everything so that you won't get sick and can properly treat and filter the water.)
Marcos assured the public that there will be an adequate supply of rice, beef, chicken, fish, and pork, but warned that vegetable production would be severely impacted during the Super El Niño.
He encouraged the public to embrace “green revolution” by growing their own crops at home, similar to what was done during the pandemic.
Territorial waters

On maritime aggression, Marcos expressed grave concern over the recent interference by the China Coast Guard in a medical emergency evacuation for a Philippine Navy personnel aboard BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal.
The President acknowledged that an escalation is taking place in the West Philippine Sea between the Philippines and China.

“Unfortunately, there really is an escalation. There are more stated requirements [and] permissions. In my own property, you’re going to tell me what I am allowed and not allowed to do? Within my own territory? Dagat namin to eh (this is our sea),” Marcos said.
Proposed social media ban
Meanwhile, regarding a proposed social media ban for minors, Marcos said his office is still assessing the decision.

He pointed out that while other countries have implemented similar measures, the government is studying whether it will be effective or if it might make monitoring harder because children would simply hide their activity.

“Tinitignan namin kung tama ba... But there’s also one thing that comes after it na 'pag binan mo [ay] itatago nung bata. So hindi mo ngayon alam na that kid is going onto that site reading about this, is getting groomed. Maybe that's the hard question. Maybe it's better if we know kahit na they are not doing the right thing, turuan natin,” Marcos explained.

(We are looking into whether this is the right approach... But there is also the issue that if you ban it, children will just hide it. Then you won't know that a child is accessing that site, reading content, or being groomed. Maybe that's the hard question. Perhaps it's better if we know, even if they aren't doing the right thing, so we can guide them.)
The Senate on Friday approved the Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces or Smart Kids Act, a bill seeking to ban minors from having social media accounts.

Under the bill, children aged 17 and below are restricted from having access to harmful digital applications and websites. Existing accounts belonging to minors will be disabled or suspended, and they will be barred from creating new ones. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Student lay in wait for housemate before stabbing him 30 times, Bristol court hears
articles.summary:
Zack Coughlan is accused of murdering Jamie Collins, who he studied with at the University of the West of England

A university student lay in wait for his housemate to return home before…

blocks.text: A university student lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times, a murder trial has been told.

Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed all in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near the University of West England in Bristol, where both studied robotics.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April after returning from campus on his bike, Bristol crown court heard.
Coughlan then allegedly cycled away on the bike, dumped it at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing into a pond.
He returned home to the house they shared in Filton, south Gloucestershire, at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends, the court was told.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, said: “A few hours later he decided it was time to call the police and pretend that he had just found his friend’s body in the garden.
“At about 2am – eight hours later – the defendant called 999. He said that his friend had been stabbed. They told him to do CPR until paramedics arrived and he told them that he was.”
He told police he had noticed the back gate was open, went outside and found Collins’s body.
The court heard the attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house, which Coughlan showed officers who initially treated him as a witness.
Coughlan had injuries to his hands but he said he had hurt himself when he fell while climbing trees.

Vaitilingam said that as evidence against Coughlan mounted, he went from being a witness to a suspect. He now accepted he had killed Collins but denied murder. He said he “lost his self-control” when he carried out the attack, the barrister said.
The jury was told that Coughlan and Collins were both final year students and lived together in a house owned by the defendant.
Vaitilingam said there had been disagreements between the pair about paying rent and whether Coughlan was charging too much, but they appeared to have been resolved.

“There was nothing that any friends were aware of that seemed to be a significant problem,” he said. They hung out together both in person and online, they did gaming together, they went out together, entirely normal student life.”
The trial continues.

articles.title: More part-time bosses and co-CEOs could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s pay gap
articles.summary:
Uneven caring responsibilities combined with a lack of flexible work options have prevented women from staying in senior positions, research suggests

  • Get our

blocks.text: More part-time bosses and “co-CEOs” could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s gender pay gap, the federal government’s Workplace Gender Equality Agency says.
WGEA warned resistance to gender equality was growing and urged employers to make management more flexible to reduce the gender pay gap, where women earn $0.79 for every $1 a man makes on average.

WGEA and Curtin University research on Tuesday found women were reaching senior positions but were more likely to leave, widening the pay gap and contributing to under-representation in high-paying and senior roles.
Full-time women were promoted more often than men in 2024-25, according to the report’s analysis of WGEA data covering 5.4 million employees.
But men were slightly more likely to be promoted to management positions and women who reached management positions were more likely to resign than their male counterparts, at 13.8% compared to 12%.
WGEA’s chief executive, Christine Castley, said uneven caring responsibilities combined with a lack of flexible work options had prevented women from staying in senior positions.
“There is very much an embedded idea that management roles can never be part-time, and probably what flows from that is most flexible arrangements don’t apply to management roles,” Castley said.
Most women still either stop working or work part-time after having their first child, according to the report’s analysis of Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (Hilda) data.
Leadership could be dominated by men even in industries where most workers were women, the report found.

In the health care and social assistance sector, women made up three-quarters of the workforce but about half of CEO positions. Women accounted for just one in five board chairs or chief executives of Australian companies.
Castley said employers could think creatively about reforms to keep women in senior roles, including allowing grandparents to access carer’s leave or rostering to fit school drop-off and pickup.
“We’re seeing increasingly the use of – even at the CEO level – co-CEOs, who are essentially job sharing a role.”
The report found that just 13.2% of organisations designed management roles for part-time work but those that did saw significantly higher promotion rates for female part-time non-managers.
Employers with flexible work strategies tended to employ more women at every level of senior management.
after newsletter promotion
Dr Silvia Salazar, a report co-author, said parents sharing care responsibility would also play a role.
Women accounted for 80% of people taking primary carer parental leave in 2024-25 and were more likely to quit their job while on parental leave than men.
The report found 33% employers were not funding additional paid parental leave.
“Employers cannot determine how care is divided at home, but they can help make sure that becoming a parent does not mean stepping off the path to career progression,” Salazar said.
Workplace equality metrics have improved in recent years but policies addressing gendered inequality have faced growing hostility, especially among Australian youth.
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has said the gender pay gap is due to women taking time off but employers should not have to pay for parental leave.
Castley said the agency aimed to provide objective data in the face of growing scepticism over gender equity.
“Certainly many people who have worked in this space have a bit of a sense that the conversation’s moved a few steps backwards from where it was,” Castley said.
“We have made really good progress over the last 40 years or so in this context, but now there is a narrative that seems to be pulling that progress backwards, at least in a narrative sense.”

articles.title: Rescued turtles return home after NSW government cut flows to wetland
articles.summary:
Environmental water to the area was halted after a complaint from a private landholder, leading to the deaths of wildlife and sheep

  • Get our
articles.byline: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Freshwater turtles rescued from a dried-up water hole in western New South Wales after the state government cut environmental water to the area are being returned home.
Late last month, 10 broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released back into the Gingham water hole in the state’s Gwydir region.
In what the environment minister, Penny Sharpe, described as a “remarkable conservation outcome”, 281 eggs from rescued turtles are also incubating at Taronga zoo in Dubbo.
The rapidly drying water hole was the site of a rescue mission in April after University of New England scientists raised the alarm that an “incomprehensible” environmental catastrophe was unfolding.

blocks.caption: The dried-up Gingham water hole in April after environmental flows were stopped. Photograph: NSW Government

blocks.text: WaterNSW had stopped environmental flows to the area, after a complaint from a private landholder, leading to the deaths of turtles, birds, frogs and sheep.
Environmental flows refer to water released by the government from dams and tributaries into rivers and ecosystems to maintain or restore their health.

The situation sparked outcry after scientist Deb Bower spoke publicly to Guardian Australia, with footage taken by NSW Greens water spokesperson Cate Faehrmann showing the researchers digging through mud to find surviving turtles.

Thirty-nine turtles were taken into care at Taronga zoo in Dubbo. In May, the government expedited legislation to clearly protect WaterNSW from liability claims when delivering environmental flows, and the water was turned back on.
Six months on, the Gingham water hole is full once more and the first group of 13 surviving turtles have been returned to their habitat.

blocks.caption: Twenty-four turtles still in care are expected to return to the water hole by the end of the year. Photograph: NSW Government

blocks.text: “That’s what we work for as conservation scientists – to be able to get animals back into the wild,” said Dr Phoebe Meagher, a wildlife conservation officer at Taronga Conservation Society.
Meagher said of the 39 turtles, two had to be humanely euthanised. She said the remaining 37 turtles were healthy enough to be rehabilitated.
She said the 24 turtles that were still in care were expected to return by the end of the year, pending health checks.

Many of the turtles rescued in April had been carrying eggs. Meagher said zoo staff made a decision to induce the animals for welfare reasons and 281 eggs were being housed in incubators, with the hatchlings expected early next year.
Meagher said not all of the eggs would hatch successfully but the zoo hoped to release any hatchlings back at the Gingham water hole when they were ready.
Photos and video of the adult turtles being released late last month showed a much healthier site than the parched environment that confronted researchers in May.
“When those animals got brought to us, it was a pretty dire situation,” Meagher said.
after newsletter promotion
“To be able to see those photos of how good it looks and see the turtles being released back to their home, that’s what we work for as conservation scientists
“To be able to even further boost that population with hatchlings, it’s why we do what we do.”
Sharpe said conservation “isn’t always about following a set playbook”.
“Sometimes a crisis creates an opportunity to do something truly groundbreaking,” she said.
“By rescuing these turtles and safeguarding more than 250 eggs, we’ve turned a potential loss into a remarkable opportunity for species recovery.”
Faehrmann said she was “incredibly relieved to see that some of the turtles have started to be released back into the Gwydir wetlands”.
“This is a good news story but not because of the efforts of the government, despite what their media release says,” she said.
“It wasn’t until the Guardian published its story with the footage I provided of the turtles being dug up out of the mud that the government swung into action.
“It shouldn’t have taken the courage of the UNE researchers and a viral video to get the government to act, but that’s what was needed.”
She said she had been “kept up at night” wondering how many other wetlands and wildlife were suffering because there was not enough water for the environment.
Faehrmann recently returned from a trip to the Ramsar-listed Macquarie Marshes and said the area desperately needed more flows.

articles.title: Julie Inman Grant may be able to limit Australians seeing a livestreamed US execution – but it could start a diplomatic incident
articles.summary:
A history of tech giant legal challenges and US political criticism shows there’s no easy solution for the eSafety commissioner

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s online safety regulator has a few levers to limit the public seeing the US’s planned livestream of an execution, but history suggests it will lead to a very public fight.
The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced last week the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would be livestreamed when the military execution is carried out in early December.

The Greens have called on the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the Albanese government to ensure that the event – if it goes ahead and is livestreamed – is not seen by Australians on TV or their devices.

The eSafety commissioner, under the Online Safety Act, has powers to order platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and X to block Australians from accessing posts that contain content deemed to be “refused classification” under Australian classification law.

The classification of such extreme violent material is typically applied to content online of terror attacks and other terror-related content, but it could be applied to clips of the video of the public execution after the fact.

While some companies like Meta will probably apply their own terms of service and prevent the distribution of the video, history suggests others will take a stand that the video should remain on their platforms.
X has given no indication whether it will allow such videos, but the platform owned by Elon Musk has a long history of legal challenges against eSafety when it comes to this sort of content.

In 2024, X was successful in allowing footage of the stabbing of a Sydney bishop in his church in 2024 to remain available to Australians – the platform even recruited the bishop, Mar Mari Emmanuel, to argue to the court to allow the footage to stay online.

Most recently, X won an appeal to the classifications review board to have the classification of the video of the assassination of rightwing influencer Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University downgraded from RC to R18+, after eSafety ordered the removal of clips of the assassination last year.
It also won a similar case to reduce the rating of videos of the attack on Iryna Zarutska on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina in August last year down to R18+.

In laws passed by the former Coalition government in 2019 in the wake of the Christchurch terror attack, the eSafety commissioner also has powers to issue takedown notices to websites hosting footage that, among other things, depicts “actual violent crime such as murder, attempted murder, rape, torture”.
These laws were developed with the view to block streaming of terror attacks, but could have wider applications for state-sponsored violence such as executions.

The eSafety commissioner last used these powers in 2022 to order websites to remove videos and related materials of the Buffalo, New York terrorist attack in 2022. It can also declare an “online crisis event” and order internet service providers such as Telstra and Optus to block sites hosting the content, but this power has yet to be used.
The ISPs complied with eSafety’s request to block sites hosting the Christchurch attack in 2019 before the parliament had passed the laws.
after newsletter promotion

Such a move – particularly if focused on large social media platforms, or potentially sites owned by the Trump administration – may lead to a domestic firestorm among conservative media as well as a potential diplomatic incident, and may not be the regulator’s preferred option – especially given it has not been used before.

Last, there is the potential to seek penalties against platforms that fail to detect and remove violent material from their platform. The regulator is now testing this law out with messaging platform Telegram, which eSafety has alleged failed to remove some content that included executions conducted by terrorist groups.
The eSafety commissioner is seeking fines of up to A$54.6m, and the hearing for the case is set down for February next year.

The other factor to consider is the laser focus some in the US already have on Inman Grant. Her term is up in January next year, and Inman Grant has previously said she will not seek another term, but Trump-aligned politicians such as the Republican congressman Jim Jordan have labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns” and claimed she has threatened American speech on social media platforms.
Inman Grant has rejected the claims, and she declined an invitation to speak before a US congress hearing at the time.
If Inman Grant bears the responsibility for decisions around whether Australians can see the livestreamed execution, it will likely provoke a new round of criticism.

The regulator has not indicated what it would do in the event the execution is livestreamed, but the history of legal challenges and attention from the right of politics in the US suggests no easy solution in the eSafety toolkit – short of ministerial intervention.

articles.title: Australian democracy campaigner detained in Vietnam on alleged terrorism offences uncontactable, wife says
articles.summary:
Tran Hiep spent his 51st birthday alone in a notorious detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City after his sudden arrest last month

  • Get our

blocks.text: Tran Hiep spent his 51st birthday alone in a notorious detention centre in Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City after his sudden arrest last month.

The Melbourne-based Vietnamese-Australian democracy campaigner hasn’t been heard from since mid-September when Vietnamese authorities detained him for alleged terrorism and forging identity documents.
The alarm was first raised by his wife, Chloe Dang, when Hiep failed to board his flight from the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on 18 September where he was meeting with human rights defenders.
For nearly a fortnight, Hiep had apparently vanished. Then the Vietnamese authorities confirmed he was in jail, awaiting trial.

More than three weeks later, Dang has been told by Australian authorities Hiep is being held in the B34 pre-trial detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, known for alleged human rights abuses against political prisoners.
“I will not stop worrying until I hear from him or see him with my own eyes,” Dang said.
“Last week, he had to spend his birthday alone in detention. We always do everything together, so the thought of that is truly heartbreaking for me.”
Dang wants his immediate and unconditional release.
Not the only detainee
Hiep is the latest Australian human rights campaigner to be detained in Vietnam.

Vietnamese-born Australian, Chau Van Kham, was arrested in Vietnam in January 2019 and sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment on “financing terrorism” charges over his membership of the pro-democracy group Viet Tan. He was released after four years in 2023.
Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, is also accused of being a member of Viet Tan – which Vietnam describes as a terrorist group.

Human Rights Watch has previously described Viet Tan as “an opposition political party … which operates openly and lawfully in many countries including Australia, but which Hanoi arbitrarily labels ‘terrorist’”.

According to a Vietnamese government statement, Hiep was arrested entering Vietnam from the Cambodian border along with another human rights activist, Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.

blocks.caption: Hiep Tran, and his wife, Chloe Dang. Photograph: Chloe Dang

blocks.text: A third person, Thai Cong Truong Son, was also arrested. Cambodian authorities have since denied any involvement in the arrest or detainment of the three men, who, they say, were intercepted at the My Quy Tay border crossing.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing the family with consular assistance but won’t comment on his case due to privacy obligations.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said she had made personal representations regarding Hiep’s case but would be “careful what I say publicly”.
“We know that different political regimes in the region have very different approaches to individual freedom and political freedom to that Australia takes,” Wong told ABC on Friday.
after newsletter promotion
‘Worsening human rights situation’
Human rights advocates are concerned Australia’s silence in the public arena is the wrong approach while Hiep remains uncontactable, and his condition unknown.
Kyinzom Dhongdue, Amnesty International Australia’s strategy and efficacy manager, said the human rights group was “increasingly concerned about the worsening human rights situation in Vietnam”.

Dang, as well as Hiep’s lawyer Alison Battisson, Amnesty, Human Rights Watch, and other groups, believe Hiep was abducted by Vietnamese authorities while in Cambodia. If so, his arrest would be a violation of international law.
“This is an egregious case of transnational oppression in which an Australian citizen has been kidnapped from a third country – Cambodia – and forcibly taken to Vietnam,” Battisson claimed.
Both Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities deny this happened.
Dhongdue said the Australian government should demand an independent investigation, noting previous cases.
“I think the government really needs to speak out publicly, privately, at the highest level, because keeping it quiet doesn’t help,” Dhongdue said.
Kylie Moore-Gilbert was held in Iranian detention from September 2018 for 804 days until her eventual release in November 2020.
Moore-Gilbert said the Australian government’s decision not to make her detainment public until 2019 led to her being sentenced to 10 years’ jail for espionage in a secret trial.
She hoped it would not be the same for Hiep.
“I would really hope that they would learn the lessons from that experience with that detention and apply them in order to act more expeditiously in [Hiep’s] case,” Moore-Gilbert said.
“Keeping that media spotlight on him will hopefully protect him a bit from some of the worst excesses of that regime.
“We need to put our foot down as a country … we really need to send a strong signal to Vietnam that [his arrest is] unacceptable and that we will accept nothing less than his immediate freedom.”

articles.title: Rent-tech platforms sidestepping credit card surcharge ban with new fees and paid ‘memberships’
articles.summary:
Tenants encouraged to seek free options after online property platforms respond to Reserve Bank’s credit card payment reform

  • Get our

blocks.text: Online property management platforms are charging renters new fees or pushing them on to paid “memberships” to avoid processing costs associated with card payments in the wake of the ban on surcharges.
Tenants have been encouraged to challenge or bypass additional fees charged by so-called rent-tech platforms, including in Victoria, where fees on rent payments are banned.
At least 1.2m rent payments each month are made on the platforms in Australia, typically at the instruction of property managers and often with an extra transaction fee.
Following the Reserve Bank’s ban on surcharging from 1 October, the rent-tech platform OurProperty told Guardian Australia it had stopped accepting direct card payments across the country.

OurProperty’s founder, Russell Burstow, said it previously charged a 1.95% surcharge. It would now route payments through Pay4it, a platform Burstow founded in August which charged its own 1.95% “service fees”.

Burstow said OurProperty passed the cost on to tenants as the alternatives were to lift costs of real estate agencies or stop accepting cards, which he said would put customers who relied on credit cards into rental arrears.
“There’s no way that the agency would absorb that sort of money,” Burstow said. “They would just pass it on to the landlord, who would just push the rent up.”
Burstow said OurProperty and Pay4it were not making more money out of the new arrangements and would start losing money unless the Visa and Mastercard networks dropped their processing fees.

Victoria will outright ban rental providers and real estate agents from charging people fees to pay their rent or submit tenancy applications later this month, after prohibiting rent-tech companies from doing so in March.

In that state, OurProperty will introduce a new system of “memberships” on Tuesday. It will waive the “service fees” associated with paying by card via Pay4it for tenants who take out a “platinum” membership, which costs 1.95% of their monthly rent.
Curtis Thomson, chief executive of OurProperty, said the Victorian memberships included new app features and did not replace old card surcharges.

He said Victorian tenants would by default be granted a “silver” membership, meaning their real estate agency would have to cover the fees it charged for direct debit and automated bank transfer. Direct debit and automated transfer will still incur fees on OurProperty outside Victoria.
A Melbourne tenant using the platform, Hazel Kearns-Rees, said she was first notified on Thursday that she would have to opt out of her new membership.
“The framing of the costs as memberships … and the fact that all free options are made to be deliberately very difficult and inconvenient feels pretty unethical,” Kearns-Rees said.
“The ways that they are making it specifically difficult to make a fee-free rent payment is really disgusting, especially in a cost-of-living crisis.”
Seek advice first
The loss of card surcharging has upended rental payments as businesses find alternatives or workarounds to avoid footing the transaction cost themselves.

Another platform, Ailo, has also swapped card surcharges for paid memberships. Ben White, the company’s founder, said customers would be paying the same or less overall and fee-free options had not changed.

The biggest platform, DEFT, has blocked debit and credit cards altogether. Its owner, Macquarie Bank, said card accounted for just 2% of the 1.2m rent payments it processed each month and tenants could still pay via BPAY, direct debit and PayID.
after newsletter promotion

Dr Fengfei Li, a senior lecturer in finance at Deakin University, said the surcharge reforms were meant to change prices and renaming a charge to a “membership” fee was not necessarily permissible under the ban, even if bundled with other services.
“The important questions are what the fee actually pays for, how it is calculated, and whether tenants are effectively required to pay it to access card payments,” Li said.

“Consumers do not simply have to accept a new fee at face value. They can first ask the platform to explain the charge and, where the service is optional, decline it and use an available fee-free payment method.”

Every Australian state requires that tenants be offered at least one fee-free way to pay rent and some have banned all fees on payments. In New South Wales, the office of the fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, urged worried renters to seek the regulator’s help.
“We encourage anyone who is concerned they have been misled into paying memberships or other fees while paying their rent to get in contact with NSW Fair Trading,” a spokesperson said.

A Victorian customer – who lives in a build-to-rent property in Melbourne’s Parkville run by the property management company UKO – successfully challenged a new payment fee they were recently charged.

UKO wrote to tenants in August to “strongly encourage” them to sign up to a new payment portal operated by the property management software company Yardi, and that they should set up recurring rent payments.
Tenants claim they were not told they would be charged a 1.99% “service fee”. The Guardian sought comment from UKO.
One tenant raised the fee with the state government regulator after noticing they had been charged an additional $54.47 on top of their monthly payment.

They were charged the fee despite Victoria’s new protections around third-party rent-payment fees. When they queried the fee with Consumer Affairs Victoria and their building manager, they were told it had been a card payment processing fee and that it would be removed from 30 September.
“I don’t know whether the surcharge would have been removed … if I hadn’t raised it,” they said.
The tenant said they were concerned other renters may be unaware they were paying similar fees.
Contacted for comment, a Consumer Affairs Victoria spokesperson said the regulator “takes reports of misconduct seriously and will investigate and take action where necessary”.

articles.title: Cyber-attack like OpenAI Medicare breach ‘seems likely’ in UK, says minister
articles.summary: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by AI agent

blocks.text: An AI-driven cyber-attack like the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister.
Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity.

In a speech on Monday, Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK.
“It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.”
Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that was not authorised to have.
“The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said.

Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI.

Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesday into the issue. Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete.
Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability.

“I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said.
The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat.
after newsletter promotion

“And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: Listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviours. And if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.”
Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year.
“We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.

articles.title: Less than 50% of 47k public schools have CCTV cameras -DepEd
articles.summary: The Department of Education on Monday reported that less than 50% of the 47,000 public schools in the country have CCTV cameras installed despite numerous violent incidents in the past months.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 9:49pm
The Department of Education on Monday reported that less than 50% of the 47,000 public schools in the country have CCTV cameras installed despite numerous violent incidents in the past months.
DepEd said this during the deliberations of the House Committee on Basic Education and Culture on various bills on school security and safety.

"After Tacloban, nag-conduct ang DepEd ng security and safety audit. During that June audit, lumalabas na may 36% of our schools ay mayroon nang CCTV. Pero nag-run tayo ng another round of audit," DepEd Assistant Secretary Roger Masapol said.
"Ngayon, nasa 49% na po ng schools natin ang mayroon nang CCTV cameras," he added.

(The DepEd conducted a security and safety audit after the Tacloban incident. The June audit showed that 36% of our schools already have CCTV. We ran another audit, and it showed 49% of our schools now have CCTV cameras.)
Masapol said he estimates all schools will have CCTV cameras by 2028.
The DepEd's recommendation on how many CCTV cameras should be installed in schools depends on the schools' enrollment.
For small schools with 500 students, at least five to 10 cameras are recommended.
For medium schools with 501 to 1,000 students, the DepEd's recommendation is 10 to 15 CCTV cameras.
For schools with more than 1,000 students, the DepEd recommends at least 20 CCTV cameras.
DepEd officials reported that less than half of all public schools have security guards.
They recommended that enrollment be a factor in the number of security guards assigned per school.
House Committee on Education chairman Pasig City Rep. Roman Romulo said it should be based on the number of entrances and exits of the school.

The National Youth Commission, however, emphasized that ensuring the security and safety of students does not end with erecting perimeter fences, putting metal detectors, and assigning security guards to schools.

"Hardening school infrastructure without healing the halls through mental health, threat assessment, and student support will only transform our learning into places of intimidation," NYC Executive Director and COO Atty. Carl Vincent Quitoriano told the committee.
Quitoriano cited a Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 finding that shows that 43% of girls and 53% of boys in the Philippines experience bullying regularly.
He added that the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2) noted that incidents of bullying may be underreported for fear of retaliation.

He added that "the National Youth Commission's 5th National Youth Assessment Study or NYAS revealed that 50.5% of surveyed youth experienced mental health distress and an alarming 31% reported suicidal ideation."

"In NYC's 2026 policy research and legislative agenda or PRLA, rising youth mental health issues rank as the number 1 urgent concern under health, while insecurity in schools and online spaces rank among the top peace and security concerns," Quitoriano added.
The NYC recommended five non-negotiable provisions that should be included in the bill that Congress will approve.

These are to professionalize school security officers with child protection training, behavioral threat assessment and non-punitive tip lines, mandating a minimum ratio of licensed guidance counsellors or school psychologists and establishing cluster-based itinerant mental health teams for rural and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, trauma-informed emergency drills and 15-minute parental notification, and youth co-governance in school safety.
DepEd said it is targeting to fill up 10,000 positions for guidance counselors before the end of the year. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme
articles.summary: US officials had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to Álvaro Pulido's arrest.

blocks.text: A Colombian man wanted for allegedly laundering money that had been illegally syphoned off a Venezuelan government welfare plan has been detained in the United States.

The US Department of Justice said Álvaro Pulido, 62, had been arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation on Sunday, but did not provide further details as to how he ended up in US custody.
Pulido had been in jail in Venezuela since March 2023 accused of diverting profits from the state-run oil company PDVSA.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and State Department had been offering a reward of $10m (£7.5m) for information leading to his arrest.
He is due to appear in court on Tuesday, according to a statement released by the US Attorney's Office.
Pulido's arrest comes just two months after Alex Saab, another Colombian businessman with close ties to the Venezuelan government, pleaded guilty to money laundering charges in a US court.

The US State Attorney's Office said that Pulido had been charged in two separate federal indictments "involving the alleged laundering of more than $2bn (£1.5bn) in connection with Venezuelan government bribery schemes".
US prosecutors say Pulido, along with four other co-defendants, bribed Venezuelan government officials to secure contracts to provide poor Venezuelans with food and medicine.
They accuse Pulido of wildly overcharging the Venezuelan government and laundering the profits through bank accounts abroad, including in the US.
They also allege that Pulido worked with Alex Saab to launder $350m from a separate bribery scheme involving Venezuela's currency exchange system using bank accounts in Florida.
Until recently, Saab was a powerful figure in the Venezuelan government with close ties to the then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, who named him minister of industry in 2024.
However, after Maduro was seized by US forces in a raid on Caracas in January and taken to New York to stand trial on drug-trafficking charges, Saab's fate quickly changed.
Less than two weeks after Maduro was seized, the new US-backed interim government of Venezuela sacked Saab from his post as minister, and in May it extradited him to the US.
Last month, Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada placed on 90-day preventive suspension anew
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has placed Sen. Jinggoy Estrada under preventive suspension in connection with the plunder and graft charges he"s facing related to his alleged involvement in the…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 9:45pm

The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has placed Sen. Jinggoy Estrada under preventive suspension in connection with the plunder and graft charges he’s facing related to his alleged involvement in the flood control projects scandal.

It was the second 90-day preventive suspension Estrada has received since the anti-graft court’s Second Division issued a similar resolution in June in connection with the graft charges pending before it.
The Fifth Division ordered that a copy of its resolution be furnished Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian through the Senate Secretary.
The Office of the Senate President was requested to inform the tribunal of its action within five days upon receipt of the resolution.

The Fifth Division in September affirmed its decision in July denying Estrada’s motion to fix bail in the P573-million plunder case he is facing over his alleged involvement in the flood control mess, citing lack of merit.
The court on September 3 said Estrada’s appeal “failed to demonstrate any substantial error of fact or law.”

“Accused Estrada’s motion for reconsideration places considerable emphasis on circumstances which, according to him, establish that he poses no risk of flight. He repetitively points to his incumbency as a Senator, his long tenure in public service, and his history of compliance with this court’s travel conditions. The court does not disregard these, but they do not answer the main issue presently confronting the court,” the Sandiganbayan said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say

A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a…

blocks.text: A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal.

Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there.
The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate.

As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper.

As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties.

Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative.

The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling.

In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage.

He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team.
Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations.

Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.”

Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”.

Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”.

The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer.

Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor.
The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures.

Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law. The matter remains under police investigation.

Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman.

Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”.

He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday.

blocks.caption: Left to right: George Cottrell’s then girlfriend Georgia Toffolo, Chris Bruni-Lowe, Cottrell, an unidentified man, Christopher Harborne and Nigel Farage pictured together in December 2022.

blocks.text: Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.
In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pictured around a restaurant table in May 2023 from left: Nigel Farage, Chris Bruni-Lowe, George Cottrell, Neil Gallacher of gambling group Mansion Group, Philip van Scheltinga, Richard Tice, and Cottrell’s then girlfriend Georgia Toffolo. Photograph: MJ Pictures

blocks.text: Rodrigues said: “The existence of personal or social meetings involving individuals associated with the company does not establish a corporate relationship between Redfield & Wilton Strategies and Reform UK.”

While much of Redfield & Wilton’s published polling related to voter intentions in the UK and the US, sources said Bruni-Lowe had its staff develop a “dossier” on local authority performance between autumn 2024 and spring 2025.

One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services.

Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage.
The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies.

Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client.

One unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”.

The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”.
According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”.

One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”.
Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph.

Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source.
Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’
articles.summary:
‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames

Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food…

blocks.text: Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.

Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.”

The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red.

The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground carpark, a council daycare facility and community centre.

blocks.caption: The Marché des Enfants Rouges in the Marais district in Paris drew thousands of locals and tourists daily.  Photograph: Photononstop/Alamy

blocks.text: A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s.

Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000.

While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables.

The current Time Out tourist guide describes Les Enfants Rouges as “the coolest market in Paris”, while the authoritative US website Food&Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year after other food courts in London, Bangkok, Lyon and Mexico City.

Lt Col Pierre de Bouvier of the Paris fire service said much of the metal structure of the market had fallen in, and most of the stalls had gone up in flames. More than 150 firefighters and 50 fire trucks battled the blaze after being alerted at 4.15am, he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.

articles.title: Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance
articles.summary:
Researchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraft

A team of US researchers is approaching a remote Pacific atoll where they…

blocks.text: A team of US researchers is approaching a remote Pacific atoll where they suspect the famed aviator Amelia Earhart crash-landed in 1937, in the latest attempt to crack one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century.

The 17-person expedition was inspired by satellite images taken over several years showing a submerged object in the uninhabited island’s sandy lagoon – evidence dismissed by other longtime Earhart sleuths who say it is probably a fallen tree.

These researchers – led by archaeologists who raised funding from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University – hope it will instead be revealed as the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. Separate aerial footage of the area suggested the submerged object has a metallic glint, the team say.

“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” said the expedition’s leader, Richard Pettigrew, before he set sail this month. “Confirming the plane wreckage there would be the smoking-gun proof.”

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator. By that point, Earhart, 39, was already a celebrity and aviation pioneer, having broken several records including being the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight​.

Locating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held – but unproven – hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll of Nikumaroro, part of the archipelago country of Kiribati and about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

blocks.caption: A 2001 satellite images shows Nikumaroro, an uninhabited Pacific coral atoll in the Republic of Kiribati.  Photograph: REUTERS

blocks.text: They were en route to Howland Island, about 400 miles north of Nikumaroro, when their plane ran low on fuel and disappeared.

After a six-day sea voyage from Tarawa, the capital of Kiribati, the research group is expected to arrive on the uninhabited atoll on Tuesday local time and will spend several days searching for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image.
The expedition says it has been lying there for several years, and is even visible in aerial photography dating back to 1938.

Pettigrew, who heads the Archaeological Legacy Institute, a non-profit organisation, raised funds for the mission with Purdue University in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and which funded her ill-fated final flight on the modified plane she called her “flying laboratory”. The university runs an airport and opened an Amelia Earhart Terminal last year.

The expedition builds on an already large body of evidence pinpointing the atoll as the location where the aviators went down. Much of it was gathered during dozens of visits between 1989 and 2019 by teams from the US explorers group Tigher (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery).

blocks.caption: Locating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Tighar’s co-founder – and perhaps Earhart’s most well-known explorer – Ric Gillespie, said the Taraia Object was likely a dead pandanus tree, which is ​native to the area, that washed into the ​lagoon.

Gillespie, who is the author of One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy, said he and other teams had visited the exact site where the object was located in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors.

“There’s nothing there, or we would have found it,” he said in an interview this year. “If they suddenly discover that Amelia Earhart’s wreckage is there, I’ll be very surprised, but I’d be the first one to congratulate them. But I don’t think they are going to find anything.”

While Tighar agrees the Electra made an emergency landing on the atoll, they believe it was washed off a reef and now probably lies undiscovered and in pieces in deep water off the island’s western end.

Tighar’s version of the mystery was that Earhart, and possibly Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro but survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating small fish and turtles. This theory is based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and 1930s-era artefacts, such as a jar of what is believed to be cosmetics freckle cream.
The pair’s disappearance led to a large US government search, including a flyover of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
The Purdue mission says the object may not have been found by previous expeditions as it could have been covered with sand.

MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte‘s undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025 could reach as high as P1.5 billion, a forensic financial analyst testified before the Senate impeachment court on Monday, October 12.

On Day 38 of the trial, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero asked forensic financial analyst and lawyer Alex Cabrera to estimate the “maximum” or ceiling for the possible amount of Duterte’s undeclared wealth, after Cabrera described his initial P817.87-million estimate as conservative.
“Based on your expertise and review of the documents, what would be the ceiling? If this is just the bare minimum, what would be the maximum?” Escudero asked.

Cabrera said the amount could reach P1.5 billion if his computation included the P475 million in confidential funds awarded to Duterte, another P100 million in discrepancies in Anti-Money Laundering Council records, and an increase in his estimated ownership stake in Gencorp to 45%, amounting to P250 million.

“Even if we know where the confidential funds came from, their source can be explained. But if the source is illegal, the wealth also becomes unexplained, even if you know where it came from,” Cabrera said in Filipino.

The forensic financial analyst reviewed the financial, bank, corporate, and tax records of Duterte and her spouse, Manases Carpio, as a witness for the prosecution in Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Escudero, for his part, asked Cabrera whether the computation should account for taxes owed to the government on the unexplained income. The latter agreed that the corresponding tax liabilities should eventually be calculated and deducted.
“Unexplained wealth refers to the total amount of wealth. If there are payables, we should deduct those as well, and compute the taxes,” said Cabrera.

Cabrera earlier testified that his P817.87-million estimate includes undeclared income linked to Duterte’s business interests in Cale88 Foods Corp., Metro City Chow Foods Corp., and Gencorp Industries Inc. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Former Irish Olympic swimming coach and child abuser George Gibney jailed for 15 years
articles.summary:
Gibney, 78, has faced justice for abusing athletes in the 1970s and 80s after decades of effort to track and extradite him

More than half a century after he started sexually abusing…

blocks.text: More than half a century after he started sexually abusing children, and enjoyed prestige as Ireland’s Olympic swimming coach before fleeing to the United States, George Gibney has faced justice.
The 78-year-old was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison at the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday for abusing four young female athletes in the 1970s and 1980s.
It was the culmination of a decades-long effort by victims, police, journalists and others to track down and extradite Gibney from the US.
He was convicted in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape after a closely watched trial that detailed harrowing abuse.

Judge Micheál P O’Higgin called Gibney a “manipulative predator” who had insinuated himself into the lives of children under his care. “It was predatory in nature and a gross breach of trust,” he said. “He used his coaching role to access and assault defenceless children under his care.”
The judge said Gibney had once enjoyed a stellar reputation and that the sentence reflected the gravity of his offending. “From these heights he has fallen, and his reputation now lies in tatters.”
The former coach, seated in a wheelchair, showed no emotion.
Speaking to reporters outside the court, Orla Poole said she had spent “decades in silence” because of his actions. “I thought I was the only one, that somehow, I deserved what he did to me.”

blocks.caption: One of the abuse survivors, Orla Poole, speaking to the media after Gibney was sentenced at the central criminal court in Dublin. Photograph: Cillian Sherlock/PA

blocks.text: She said other survivors should know that they were not alone and could seek support. “The only guilt for what we went through lies with the convicted paedophile. When you are ready and able, unburden yourself by talking to someone from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, One In Four, a therapist, a trusted friend or even the gardaí.”

Evin Daly, a child welfare advocate who helped to find Gibney in Florida, said the sentence was vindication for Gibney’s victims. “The abuse shaped some of their lives. The guy had no conscience, in my opinion.”

Ireland had little international success in swimming in the 1980s but Gibney became a high-profile, respected figure for establishing the Trojan club in south Dublin and for coaching emerging talent at pools around the city. He was Ireland’s coach for the Olympic games in Los Angeles in 1984 and Seoul in 1988. Gibney urged his swimmers to “never give up” and to “hang in there”.

After allegations emerged that he preyed on children at pools, in his car and other locations, he was charged with 27 counts of indecency and carnal knowledge, but in 1993 the supreme court ruled that he could not face trial because of the time that had elapsed since the alleged offences, a decision that stunned his victims.

blocks.caption: Orla Poole, second right, outside the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday. Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/PA

blocks.text: Free but infamous, Gibney moved to Scotland, then the US, where he obtained a visa and built a new life, living in Colorado, California and Florida and working mostly in low-level clerical jobs.
Several journalists continued to dig into Gibney’s crimes, including Justine McCarthy of the Irish Times who wrote a 2009 book, Deep Deception.
Daly, a forensic sociologist who was then the chief executive of a child protection advocacy group called One Child International, helped the media to locate and keep tabs on Gibney.

“We provided data and resources,” said Daly, a Florida-based court consultant on child welfare cases. “At one point Gibney moved because his neighbours in the apartment complex got wind of the fact that he was an accused sex offender and they turned on him.”
In 2020 a 10-part podcast series, commissioned by the BBC and presented by Mark Horgan, titled Where is George Gibney? revived attention and scrutiny.

Four victims who were minors when they were abused made statements to Irish police between 2020 and 2022, leading to fresh charges, an extradition warrant and Gibney’s arrest and return to Ireland last year.
After the conviction in July four victims told the court of the impact of the abuse.
One said she retained “intensely personal and traumatic memories” and had harboured a “secret shame, hurt and bewilderment” for more than half a century. The abuse was a “frozen nightmare”, she said.

Another victim, who was nine at the time of the assaults, told Gibney in court that he had abused his position of trust and that her burden of shame, guilt and embarrassment was now his. Gibney had presided over “the destruction of a previously happy and healthy child” who was powerless to verbalise her torment, she said.
