articles.title: German minister quits after death of stepdaughter and political attacks
articles.summary:
Fragile coalition suffers another blow as labour minister and co-leader of SPD Bärbel Bas leaves both posts

Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats…

blocks.text: Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government.
“After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further ⁠details.

Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner,” Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”.

Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family.

Bas’s co-leader at the SPD, Lars Klingbeil, who is also Merz’s vice-chancellor and finance minister, expressed regret at her departure and slammed the sniping against her while she was mourning as “indecent”.
Klingbeil cancelled a planned trip to India to deal with the fallout from Bas’s resignation, and criticised a degradation of the national political discourse.
“We are ​competitors, and we need ​a culture ‌of debate. ​But ​we also need a culture of mutual respect,” Klingbeil told reporters.

Merz, who has been fighting for his political survival after three disastrous state elections for his CDU last month, thanked Bas for “cooperation based on trust” in government and offered his condolences.
“As a father and grandfather, I can only imagine how deeply felt this loss is for you. I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X.

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”. She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.”
The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also saw gains for the hard left.

Bas, who will remain an MP for Duisburg in the former Ruhr mining region, is a former president of the Bundestag lower house of parliament and one of the most experienced members of the Social Democrats.
Her ministry oversees large parts of Germany’s costly social welfare system, which Merz has targeted for cuts.

While a representative of the party’s left wing, Bas was widely seen as a constructive team player able to bridge the kind of implacable policy disputes that have plagued Merz’s government since its inception in May 2025.
Her absence will now be keenly felt.
after newsletter promotion

The coalition is deeply divided over plans to revive the sputtering economy, the EU’s largest, with Merz spearheading a pro-business savings drive and the SPD insisting on maintaining protections of workers’ rights and benefits.
The pension system is in particularly urgent need of reform as German society rapidly ages but plans to gradually lift the retirement age have met with angry resistance.

Approval ratings for Merz and his government have plunged over the course of the year, with voters fearing further deindustrialisation in the face of Chinese competition and steep rises in the cost of living.
Merz, a former corporate lawyer, is often perceived as haughty and out of touch, compounding his administration’s woes and giving rise to calls to replace him at the helm.
He has vowed to stay in office and fight for his policy agenda, saying it was the only way to beat back the “poison of authoritarianism” with extremists on the march.
The next general election is due in 2029 but five more state polls loom next year.
One of Merz’s cabinet ministers, Karin Prien, sounded the alarm last week, publicly calling for a change of course in the CDU away from Merz’s harsher stances and rhetoric.

“We bit our tongues for two or three years but that’s no longer an option,” the family affairs minister told Reuters ahead of a weekend party leadership meeting, referring to its centrist wing. “The ‘pure CDU’ approach (pursued by Merz) has failed.”

articles.title: Fugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery case
articles.summary:
A businessman wanted in the US for allegedly bribing top Venezuelan officials has been taken into custody

A businessman wanted for years in the

blocks.text: A businessman wanted for years in the US for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.

Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the state department had been offering a reward of up to $10m for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido, 62, was taken into US custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agencies, American officials said on Sunday.
It was unclear how Pulido ended up in US custody. He was scheduled to make his initial court appearance on Tuesday in Miami.

“His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, wrote in a social media post Sunday.

“No amount of time or distance will stop” the justice department “from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom,” he wrote.

Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge that Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the US, sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.

The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro’s vice-president. She took over as Venezuela’s acting president following the US military’s ouster of Maduro in January.

Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for more than $2bn in contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.

Prior to these alleged offenses, Pulido had a prolific history of drug trafficking, including a 1997 conviction in Italy under the alias of German Enrique Rubio, the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Florida said in a statement.

Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the US by Rodríguez in May. In September, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195m in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.

articles.title: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
articles.summary: Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.

image.caption: Zelenskyy's POW revelation at the UN has caused a major rift with SeoulImage: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.

The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.

The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.
Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.
Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.

Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.
The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.
Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine
What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy?
There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.
"The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said.

"Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North."

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

"There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.
"I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said.
Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy
Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired?
While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.
Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.
Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue.

"Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said.
"I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."

articles.title: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees
articles.summary:
Israeli PM calls for criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in Guardian-produced documentary

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s…

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.

blocks.caption: NAZA’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival last month. Photograph: Capital Pictures/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.
The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

blocks.caption: Graffiti depicting Abraham and Szor, and the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, appeared on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel, after NAZA was awarded the special jury prize at the Venice film festival.  Photograph: Amir Cohen/Reuters

blocks.text: NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

articles.title: Cyprus closer than ever to joining Schengen but political hurdles relating to the Green Line and British Sovereign Base Areas remain
articles.summary: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area. Yet questions relating to the island's division and British military bases could still complicate its path to Europe's…

image.caption: There are nine designated crossing points between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island. Pictured here: the Leda Street crossing point in NicosiaImage: Mpalis/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.

The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."

blocks.caption: Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration, Nicholas Ioannides, says Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, Europe's border-free travel zone, which covers 29 EU and non-EU countriesImage: Markus Lenhardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.

According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.

blocks.caption: The buffer zone between the two parts of the island is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP)Image: STR/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.

This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.

"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.

The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.

Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."

"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.

According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.

Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

blocks.caption: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was in Cyprus this summer in what was seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process on the islandImage: Ali Ruhluel/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.

The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

articles.title: Digger on course for $245m loss after box office collapse
articles.summary:
Estimates suggest the eco satire starring Tom Cruise could join the list of top turkeys, including Cutthroat Island and The Marvels

Digger, the ambitious eco-fable starring Tom Cruise and…

blocks.text: Digger, the ambitious eco-fable starring Tom Cruise and directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, is heading for an even worse financial outcome than previously thought, with reports suggesting it will lose around $245m (£185m), placing it among the biggest disasters in movie history.

According to a report in Variety, Digger’s estimated second weekend revenue in North America of $3.2m is a 60% drop on its opening weekend figure of $8m, meaning its current domestic gross is $14.4m, for a global total of $35.3m, with a projected final box office total of around $50m worldwide.

Though precise figures are not available, Variety estimates that Digger’s production costs are $160m-180m (well over the original budget of $125m), with another $100m spent on marketing the film. Another $15m was potentially on hand for awards-season marketing, but this is likely to be scaled back after the film’s failure. Given that cinemas keep around half the revenue of ticket sales, Variety estimates the film would need to make around $350m to cover costs. (A spokesperson for Digger’s producing studio Warner Bros, says that break-even point is $300m, suggesting a production spend of $150m.)
A $245m loss would put Digger on a par with such legendary turkeys as Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and The Marvels ($205-$250m adjusted).

Reaction to the film has likely played a key role in its underperformance, with critical opinion radically divided. In the Guardian, chief film critic Peter Bradshaw called it “an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire” in a two-star review, while Guardian Australia’s deputy culture editor Sian Cain took the opposite position, describing it as “a masterpiece”. Warner Bros, whose last release this is before its takeover by David Ellison’s Skydance, tried to play into the controversy with a post-release advertising campaign quoting its negative notices, but it seems to have had little effect.

So far, 2026 has been a disappointing year for Warner Bros, as it prepares for new ownership, with poorly performing releases such as Supergirl and The Bride! and co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy due to leave ahead of the takeover. This contrasts with a successful 2025, in which releases such as A Minecraft Movie, Sinners and F1 propelled it to the second most successful studio, behind Disney.

Elsewhere, the Aaron Sorkin-directed The Social Reckoning also failed to live up to expectations on its first weekend, taking an estimated $5.5m at the North American box office and $9m globally. The sequel to The Social Network, which stars Jeremy Strong as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and Mikey Madison as whistleblower Frances Haugen, was comprehensively beaten by Jessica Chastain horror The Other Mommy, which led the North American box office with an estimated $27.5m, part of a global take of $45.2m.

blocks.text: Federal agents searched Representative Ilhan Omar’s home Monday morning as part of a criminal fraud investigation, according to reports in the Associated Press and Fox News that cited a statement from the department of justice.
A video posted by Fox showed what appeared to be law enforcement in HSI jackets at what Fox News said was Omar’s Washington DC residence.

“Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation,” a DoJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Fox News reported based on unnamed sources familiar with the matter that agents were examining the immigration paperwork that the congresswoman’s father filled out when she was a child.
Donald Trump and key allies have accused Omar of obtaining citizenship fraudulently, fantasizing openly about denaturalizing her and expelling her from the country.

The congresswoman has consistently denied the accusations, though Trump has repeatedly made them national news with gratuitous attacks against Omar, who along with Representative Rashida Tlaib became the United States’s first Muslim congresswoman in 2019.

But even amid a presidency known for political and legal retribution against the Donald Trump’s critics, the search of Omar’s DC home just three weeks before a crucial midterm Election Day will surely lead to new accusations that Trump is using the government for his own political ends.

articles.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
articles.summary: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies

blocks.text: Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.

Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).

“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.
Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.

Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).
Woodfood built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.
This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.

Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.
after newsletter promotion

Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.
And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.
Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.
Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into fresh water and salt water varieties.

The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.

Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.

articles.summary: Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes on the northeastern city of Kharkiv. The Kremlin says it would only consider a one-day…

image.caption: At least 12 people were reportedly injured in Russian strikes on Kharkiv, according to the city's mayorImage: Andrii Marienko/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend.
Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."
There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."
Ukrainian energy facility attacked

On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.
"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
Zelenskyy: Ukraine 'will respond' if no ceasefire
Zelenskyy expressed readiness in principle to back an agreement to refrain from attacks on energy infrastructure, but said such a ceasefire must be backed up by security guarantees.
"This ceasefire, it can work, and it can ​become ⁠a major step toward ending the war if ⁠the ​Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said.
"We are waiting for the ​of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to ​see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.
"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."

French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."
The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.
The Kremlin earlier rejected ​a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by ⁠President ​Zelenskyy.
"I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.summary:
Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breach stretched defences

Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh on Monday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one dead.

The Gulf nation said it was taking the step after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.

King Khalid international airport was being kept closed to complete verification of the airport’s safety, the Saudi aviation authority said. Saudi Arabia’s military spokesperson also said further missile and drone threats had been detected.

blocks.caption: Before and after the strike as people queue up for flights at King Khalid international airport on Saturday. Photograph: Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters

blocks.text: The closure came as the country pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises.

An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.

The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014.

Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi air planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.

The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.

Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids through Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.

blocks.caption: A billboard displays an image of the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, in Sana’a, Yemen on Sunday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.

The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.

The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.

Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.

Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

articles.title: House passes P7.2-trillion 2027 budget amid pork barrel concerns
articles.summary: 'This budget is not people-centered. It is election-centered,' says Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima

blocks.text: LOWER CHAMBER. The House of Representatives Session Hall.
House of Representatives' Facebook page
'This budget is not people-centered. It is election-centered,' says Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima

items: The House of Representatives in the Philippines passed a P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, receiving 282 votes in favor amid opposition from some lawmakers and civil society groups concerned about 'pork barrel' allocations.

Critics, including several representatives, argue that the budget prioritizes election-centered spending and lacks transparency, particularly regarding social assistance programs that could be misused for political patronage.

The People's Budget Coalition has raised alarms over significant cuts to foreign-assisted projects, warning that these reductions could delay essential infrastructure developments and expose the government to additional fees.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The House of Representatives passed the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on third and final reading on Monday, October 12, amid concerns from some lawmakers and civil society organizations that the spending plan is riddled with pork barrel allocations.
The measure received 282 votes in favor, 13 against, and one abstention.

Among those who voted against the proposed budget were Dinagat Islands Representative Kaka Bag-ao, Akbayan Representative Percival Cendeña, Kabataan Representative Renee Co, Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima, Cebu City 1st District Representative Rachel del Mar, Gabriela Representative Sara Elago, Caloocan 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice, Kamanggagawa Representative Eli San Fernando, Navotas Representative Toby Tiangco, and ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio.
Most of these lawmakers flagged the huge allocation for ayuda or social assistance programs which, they say, are prone to use for patronage politics.
“This budget is not people-centered. It is election-centered,” De Lima said. The 2027 budget will be used a year before the 2028 national elections.
Erice, San Fernando, and Tiangco also flagged the lack of transparency in the budget process.
San Fernando questioned the budget amendments review committee’s meeting over its supposed executive session on Thursday, October 1.

The livestream of the hearing was supposed to start at 1 pm, but it only started at 5:07 pm. In that meeting, lawmakers allocated a bigger budget for social assistance programs and infrastructure projects.

blocks.caption: Executive session? House’s budget amendment review panel livestream delayed for hours

blocks.text: The People’s Budget Coalition (PBC), a civil society group monitoring the national budget, also criticized the proposed spending plan, warning against the use of public funds for political patronage.

These include the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations, the Department of Health’s Medical Assistance for Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients, and the Department of Labor and Employment’s Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged Workers.

The coalition also flagged a P130-billion cut in foreign-assisted projects, including the Metro Manila Subway, the North-South Commuter Railway, bypass roads, and flood mitigation projects in major river basins.

According to the coalition, these projects are backed by loans that the Philippines has already signed. Budget cuts could delay their implementation without canceling the loans, potentially exposing the government to additional commitment fees and penalties.

PBC asked President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Budget Secretary Kim de Leon, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon, Senate finance committee chair JV Ejercito, and Senate President Win Gatchalian “to check the abuses of the House.”

“We refuse to let our 2027 budget become a playground for patronage and corruption again, one year after a trillion-peso flood scandal. This is our tax. This is our vote. This is our budget,” the coalition said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why Ombudsman Remulla thinks it’s important for SC to reverse ‘main plunderer’ doctrine
articles.summary: Under the doctrine, the prosecution must name a 'main plunderer' and prove that the accused personally received or benefited from the stolen money. Remulla’s interpretation of that: 'The smarter the…

blocks.text: ANNUAL REPORT. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla delivers his first annual address as the country's top anti-graft buster on October 12, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler

Under the doctrine, the prosecution must name a 'main plunderer' and prove that the accused personally received or benefited from the stolen money. Remulla’s interpretation of that: 'The smarter the thief, the safer he is.'

items: Jesus Crispin Remulla marked his first anniversary as Ombudsman by criticizing the 'main plunderer' doctrine, which he believes hinders accountability in corruption cases.

The doctrine, established by a 2016 Supreme Court ruling, requires prosecutors to identify a 'main plunderer' and prove personal benefit from the stolen funds, complicating the prosecution of large-scale corruption.
Remulla has filed 39 flood control corruption cases and calls for a reevaluation of the doctrine, emphasizing the need for judicial independence and legislative action to address the issue.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

It’s already a year since Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla was transferred from the helm of the Department of Justice to the Office of the Ombudsman, taking the responsibility of filing cases over the flood control corruption.
But in marking his first anniversary as the Ombudsman, Remulla on Monday, October 12, could not help but criticize the “main plunderer” doctrine, which emerged from a Supreme Court ruling in 2016.
For him, that doctrine “stands in the way” of accountability and ultimately securing convictions.

Strong words from Remulla’s address: “Ang batas laban sa pandarambong ay ginawa para panagutin ang mga nagnanakaw ng bilyon-bilyon. Pero, sa doktrinang ito, ang pinakamalaking sindikato ang pinakamahirap mahuli.
“Hindi po iyan hustisya. Pananggalang po iyan.”
(The law against plunder was legislated to hold accountable those who steal billions. But with this doctrine, the biggest syndicate is the hardest to catch. That’s not justice, that’s a shield.)

The “main plunderer” doctrine emerged from former president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s SC case involving her alleged misuse of P366 million in confidential and intelligence funds of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office. In 2012, then-ombudsman Conchita Carpio-Morales charged Arroyo with plunder.
The 2016 SC decision, penned by then-justice Lucas Bersamin, acquitted Arroyo and granted her release. (Bersamin became President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s executive secretary, resigning
Remulla said that the SC ruling read into the Republic Act No. 7080 or the Anti-Plunder Act two requirements “that Congress never wrote.”
The prosecution must name a “main plunderer” and prove that the accused personally received or benefited from the stolen money.
Remulla’s interpretation of that: “The smarter the thief, the safer he is.”
“Pass the money through enough dummies, middlemen, and shell companies, and no one can be shown to have touched it,” he said. He noted that such a scheme is present in the flood control controversy.

blocks.caption: Why Ombudsman Remulla thinks it’s important for SC to reverse ‘main plunderer’ doctrine

blocks.text: Remulla’s remark came after he reported that 39 flood control cases have been filed with the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan and regional courts.

And since the Office of the Ombudsman already accomplished the “hardest part” of building cases, the next chapter lies with the courts, which they expect to be “impartial, independent, and attuned to the times.”
Remulla has repeatedly mentioned the hurdle set by the “main plunderer” doctrine.
In 2016, four justices dissented with the SC ruling to acquit Arroyo, including the introduction of two additional elements in the prosecution of plunder. For them, it was a “dangerous precedent.”

Among the dissenters, Justice Marvic Leonen wrote back then: “In doing so, this Court sets itself upon the course of encroaching on Congress’ plenary power to make laws. It also denies the State the opportunity to adequately present its case. Likewise, it unwittingly licenses the most cunning plunderers to prey upon public funds with impunity. This is not what the Anti-Plunder Law intends.”
“Kaya sinasabi ko ito nang may buong paggalang sa Kataastaasang Hukuman: panahon na para balikan ang doktrinang ito. It is time to revisit it,” Remulla said in his first annual address.
(I say this with full respect to the High Court: It’s time to revisit this doctrine.)
For now, the High Court can only act when a case comes to their table.
Lawmakers can also pass legislation that would effectively abolish the doctrine. (But do we actually expect them to make such a move?)
What’s certain for now is the Ombudsman is trying to send signals to the country’s judiciary. Are these signals being received? – Rappler.com

articles.title: NTC eyes mandatory 1-year repair or replacement warranty for refurbished gadgets
articles.summary: The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) said Monday that it is looking at requiring a mandatory one year repair or replacement warranty for refurbished phones.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 7:31pm
The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) said Monday that it is looking at requiring a mandatory one year repair or replacement warranty for refurbished phones.
The agency said that it is already drafting rules to make it more affordable and protect consumers from purchasing stolen devices.

“The proposed rules aim to ensure that refurbished devices are only sold by properly licensed dealers, legitimately-sourced, compatible with mobile network operators (MNOs) in the Philippines, properly sanitized, graded as to condition and fully functional, with a mandatory one (1)-year repair or replacement warranty to protect consumers from smuggled, improperly refurbished and unsafe units, and stolen devices,” the NTC said in a statement.

The commission earlier said that its proposed regulation is aimed at stopping unauthorized sale of stolen phones and trade of tampered devices. It conducted a public hearing on the proposed memorandum circular last September 23.

Moreover, the NTC said that only commercial sellers applying for a Dealers Permit for Used, Reconditioned, or Refurbished Mobile Devices (DPURRMD) will face strict standards, including a minimum capitalization requirement to ensure they can honor warranties.

“The requirements, including a minimum capitalization requirement, shall apply only to applicants of Dealers Permit for Used, Reconditioned, or Refurbished Mobile Devices (DPURRMD). The capitalization requirement is intended to ensure that importers and dealers of these devices only offer type-approved and properly refurbished units and are financially capable of fully standing by the warranty of each unit sold,” the NTC said.
However, the agency noted that individuals can still freely buy and sell personal devices in non-commercial quantities without restriction.
“Maari pa rin bumili o magbenta sa merkado ang mga tao ng sarili nilang gamit. Pinapalawak lang ng NTC ang options nila,” said NTC Deputy Commissioner Alvin Blanco in a statement.
The NTC will also introduce procedures for the proper recycling and disposal of unusable devices. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Tom Cruise film Digger could lose $245m at box office
articles.summary: The film dropped by around 60% in its second weekend, and could become one of Hollywood's biggest flops.

blocks.text: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance in cinemas.
Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend.
It brings Digger's total box office takings to around $35m (£26m) globally so far. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.

But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".
The film's takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.
Digger's performance is in sharp contrast to the success of IP-driven hits starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of the Top Gun and Mission: Impossible franchises.
Digger is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.
Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.
The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.
However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).
Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.

articles.title: Defense's Sison calls Cabrera's testimony 'erroneous'; Diokno counters
articles.summary: House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno and defense lead counsel Sheila Sison exchanged words after she called financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera's testimony “erroneous.”

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 7:21pm

House prosecutor Representative Chel Diokno and defense lead counsel Sheila Sison on Monday exchanged words after the latter described as “erroneous” the testimony of financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera on the supposed unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On the Day 38 of the impeachment trial, Sison gave a manifestation, saying that Cabrera was given an “extensive platform and opportunity” to give his “unbridled and erroneous conclusions of law and fact.”
Diokno moved to strike Sison’s statement, saying that it is a conclusion of law and “totally out of order.”

“It’s up to the Honorable Court to decide whether the opinion of Atty. Cabrera is acceptable or not. And it’s not in our place, whether I’m for the prosecution or for the defense, to make such irresponsible statements. I move to strike, Your Honor,” Diokno said.
Sison objected to the motion of the prosecutor.

“Well, I object to that motion, Your Honor. In fact, it came from the gentleman himself, the witness gave an opinion that in itself is proof that the witness only gave conclusions and not facts,” she said.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero intervened, ruling that Sison’s remarks remain in the records.

“Let it remain in the record, Honorable Chel… The [defense] clearly disagrees with the opinion of the expert, and from their point of view, she described it from their perspective and not necessarily the perspective of the court nor the prosecution. Then it is not per se strikable from the point of view of the court,” Escudero said.
Diokno made a counter-manifestation, expressing the view of the prosecution on the matter.
“In the view of the prosecution, the statement of the defense that the opinion is erroneous is totally out of place and has no meaning in this court,” he stressed. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Nobel memorial prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
articles.summary: American-born economists' models have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks and "smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," says Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

image.caption: The photos of Robert E. Hall, left, and Michael Woodford are shown on the screen as they are announced as the laureates of the Nobel memorial prize in economics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on Monday. (Anders Wiklund/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
American-born economists' models have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks and "smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," says Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
Economists' work has helped manage economic shocks, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences says

American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the two were being honoured for work that has helped policymakers deal with economic fluctuations.
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement.
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: "It's a tremendous honour, it's a surprise."

The Nobel memorial prize in economics is announced in Stockholm on Monday. Hall and Woodford won the prize in for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks. (Anders Wiklund/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."
'New foundation for stabilization policy'

For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest themselves and help growth get restarted.
"This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn't," said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee.

items: He won the Nobel Prize for his work understanding the brain — and his kids flipped out
Anne Carson just won the Nobel Prize for Literature. We learn more about her literary legacy

blocks.text: Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple tradeoffs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell.
But the "stagflation" of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic.
Hall and Woodford set about coming up with an improved model that took into account how consumers and businesses actually made decisions about whether to invest and spend.
"In separate contributions, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford helped build this new foundation for stabilization policy," Hassler said.

Last year, three researchers who study business innovation — including Canadian economist Peter Howitt — won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.
Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.
The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.
Nobel honours were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.7 million Cdn), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

articles.title: CBCP calls for prayer for Pope Leo XIV as he undergoes lung surgery
articles.summary: The Catholic Bishops" Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) has called on the faithful to pray for Pope Leo XIV as he prepares to undergo lung surgery.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 7:05pm
The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) has called on the faithful to pray for Pope Leo XIV as he prepares to undergo lung surgery.
CBCP President Archbishop Gilbert Garcera appealed after Pope Leo XIV announced that he would undergo surgery to remove a small lung growth found during his recent checkup.

“I ask my brother bishops and our priests to offer Holy Mass for his successful operation and speedy and complete recovery. I likewise invite our religious communities, families, and all the faithful to offer the Holy Rosary, their daily sacrifices, and acts of charity for his healing,” Garcera said in a statement.
“Let us pray that the Lord may guide his surgeons and all who care for him, sustain him with strength and peace, and restore him to health as he continues to shepherd the universal Church,” he added.
During his weekly Sunday prayer, the Pope said the growth was "well-contained" and had been spotted early. The Vatican did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant.

A nodule on the lung is a small, localized lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.
“With filial love and confidence in God’s mercy, we entrust our Holy Father to the maternal care of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Our Lady, Health of the Sick, pray for Pope Leo XIV,” Garcera said.
The Diocese of Calbayog earlier called on the people to pray for the successful surgery and speedy recovery of Pope Leo XIV.
"May the Lord guide the hands of his doctors, grant him a successful surgery, and bless him with strength, healing, and a speedy recovery," Calbayog diocese said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: This Georgia county is one of the US’s most diverse – and that could flip multiple elections
articles.summary:
Gwinnett county is home to many immigrants and other newcomers, and how it votes could be decisive for Congress

Johanna Park might just be an ambassador for Gwinnett county, Georgia, one of…

blocks.text: Johanna Park might just be an ambassador for Gwinnett county, Georgia, one of the 10 most ethnically diverse counties in the United States.

Park owns Cafe Amico at Suwanee Town Center, one of her three Italian coffee shops in the area just north of Atlanta. She was born in Korea and lived much of her life in Argentina and Peru. She’s been in Gwinnett for more than 20 years, part of an early wave of Korean immigration that’s built Korean American car dealerships, banks, insurance agencies, supermarkets and restaurants like her own. It’s also a population that’s increasing in influence and not just numbers.

In 2020, Gwinnett was 30.6% white, 27.8% Black, 23.7% Hispanic, 13.2% Asian, and 4.0% multiracial, according to the US census. About 28% of Gwinnett residents were born outside of the United States. About half of those are US citizens. Extraordinary diversity is simply a fact of life here. According to the US census diversity index, there is an 84.9% chance that two randomly selected Gwinnett residents will belong to different racial or ethnic groups.

Control of the Senate may come down to the results of Georgia’s contest between US senator Jon Ossoff and US congressman Mike Collins. And Georgia’s election may come down to a handful of places where turnout and partisan sentiment aren’t easily predicted. Gwinnett, with its surge in population, of both US-born newcomers and immigrants, may be one of those places.
Park, who has generally voted for Democrats, has little good to say about the economy or the Trump administration.

“They’re deporting all of the Hispanic people from here, left and right,” Park said. With little media fanfare, ICE began a “shadow surge” of arrests in August. Called “Operation Safe Community”, the agency detained more than 1,000 immigrants across metro Atlanta, disproportionately targeting immigrant-heavy communities along Buford Highway, Norcross and other parts of Gwinnett county.

blocks.caption: A resident and child walk near the Lawrenceville Lawn park in Lawrenceville. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: “And not only are they deporting them back to their country, but also they are deporting them to … to south[ern] Africa? I don’t know where … And who’s paying for all of this? You know, probably you and I, with the tax money.”

“Illegal immigration has always been a thing, but why are we are so adamant about kicking everybody out when they are the hardest working people here, and they help overall with the economy?” she asked.

Park noted that Gwinnett’s immigrant community tends to be politically split between Republicans and Democrats. While the county fields more Asian American Democratic elected officials such as Akbar Ali in Lilburn, others such as Buford’s Soo Hong have been elected as Republicans. The idea of “Asian Americans” as a single voting bloc ignores nuances. Vietnamese American voters tend to be more Republican, while Indian American voters tend to be more Democratic. But neither party owns their loyalty.
Park thinks this divide “will remain, always. It’s deeply rooted. Especially the business owners are mostly pro-Republicans because of the benefits and the tax cuts and what not.”
Their children, however, may be another matter. They are often splitting with their parents, driven left with the broader trend of highly educated Americans siding with Democrats.

Elliot Kim, general manager of Suwanee Frame & Art, said: “I’m Korean. My parents live here as well, and typically that generation of Koreans and maybe a little bit younger than them stay pretty Republican and conservative because they stay close to the church. That’s what they relate to. But myself and my brother probably lean a little bit more to the left.”

Immigration has been one driver of the county’s explosive growth. Its extraordinary school system is another. US News and World Report ranked the Gwinnett School of Mathematics, Science and Technology as the top high school in Georgia and seventh nationally.

It is also far and away the largest school district in Georgia, with more than 180,000 students. Even as public school enrollment falls across America, parents around Atlanta have been voting with their feet by moving to Gwinnett. That growth - not the war, not gas prices, not even Trump - might be the key political issue for Gwinnett voters. Though housing starts have fallen since the early 2000s boom, the county has been absorbing more than 10,000 new residents a year since.

blocks.caption: Voters cast their ballots in Gwinnett County in November 2024. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Take Suwanee, on the purple fault line between football-obsessed Buford near the Mall of Georgia to its north and Duluth, where the storefront signs alternate between English, Spanish and Korean, to its south.

Kim, a graduate of Gwinnett’s vaunted public schools, is concerned that the school system today isn’t rigorous enough for his daughter, taking issue with how little homework is assigned and how often students are permitted to retake tests.
after newsletter promotion

“I mean the principal was going on and on about how Roberts [elementary school] is award-winning, best in state all this. And I’m like, how are these metrics even being formed here?” Kim said. “I am so unimpressed about what they’re learning, and maybe is that just me getting old and wanting my kids to have the amount of strife that I did going through school.”

Thirty years ago, Suwanee’s town common was a cow pasture, a million-dollar home was a rumor and apartments were the punchline to a joke about Atlanta. Today, Suwanee’s town center is a model of suburban mixed-use development ringed with condominiums, and local property values are closer to Boston’s than Atlanta’s. Its population has increased fivefold since 1996.

“My neighborhood is kind of in a bubble, I’m just going to say,” said Kristina Lindsey, a Democratic activist from Suwanee. “We have money. And so our neighborhood is not as concerned with what’s happening to maybe some people in southern Gwinnett, right? Or the gas prices or our grocery prices, right? … It does not affect us the same way it does someone who’s living paycheck to paycheck and doesn’t have an emergency fund.”
She stood on the green at Suwanee with a group of about 20 people waving anti-Trump protest signs at a weekly demonstration.

“I feel a moral obligation to be out here to be visible,” Lindsey said. “And so that other people who might share the same values as me see that we have the courage to be out here and make some noise.”

For all of America’s focus on Georgia’s swing voters with the US Senate on the line, Gwinnett Democrats may be more motivated to flip control of the state legislature. Republicans have control of Georgia’s house chamber by a 10-vote margin. Gerrymandering protects some Republicans, but the vulnerable seats are in places like Gwinnett. Republican Matt Reeves represents part of Suwanee, along with some points north. He held on to his state house seat in 2024 by 621 votes on 29,003 ballots cast, and faces a rematch against Michelle Kang, an attorney and Korean American immigrant.

There is little Republican red meat, culture war fodder, in his rhetoric. He talks about affordability – property tax relief, lowering insurance prices, and pushing for a statewide referendum for senior homestead tax exemptions.

“Here’s the thing in Gwinnett county: we are the battleground. We have competitive seats,” Reeves said. “So I’ve brought my A-game every day for the last two years. And I’ve been saying affordability for at least the last two years, probably even before that, and I’m glad that the national conversation has caught up with that because we’ve got to deliver savings, for our people to have more money in their pocket.”

State senator Adrienne White Carden heard much the same from voters as she knocked on doors. The longstanding Democratic political activist is married to a Gwinnett county commissioner and no stranger to retail campaigning. She won a special election by a 51-49 margin earlier this year in Gwinnett, serving in a temporary role until January.

“I think people are still definitely concerned about the shenanigans that Trump is running, but at the same time, they’re more interested in what’s happening here at home,” Carden said. “You know, costs definitely came up, whether it be gas pump prices or, to be honest, as the wife of a county commissioner, those who knew I was his wife – which was many people – always had a message for Commissioner Kirkland Carden about property taxes.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte, husband's 'unexplained wealth' could reach P1.5B --witness
articles.summary: The unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, could reach P1.5 billion at the maximum and P817 million at the minimum, lawyer and certified public accountant…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 6:52pm

The unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, could reach P1.5 billion at the maximum and P817 million at the minimum, lawyer and certified public accountant Alex Cabrera said Monday.

The prosecution’s witness made the testimony during Day 38 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President, assuring that his team did not make any double recording or double entry in its forensic investigation of the Vice President and her husband’s bank records, bank transactions, income tax returns, financial statements and other corporate records.

“I did not include confidential funds, which is P475 million. Our discrepancy with AMLC, if we are not going to be conservative, would be P100 million. For GenCorp. [undeclared sales], if we use 45%, that would be P250 million. So P350 million plus P475 million is P700 million,” Cabrera said when asked by Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero what his estimates would be, ceiling-wise, rather than the conservative estimate which is just at P817 million in total.
Asked what would be the ceiling amount, Cabrera said, “P1.5 billion.”
Asked by Escudero whether the amount will go down if the couple accounts for tax dues, Cabrera answered in the affirmative.
“If there are payables, we will deduct that from that (P1.5 billion) amount,” Cabrera said.
Cabrera also assured that his findings of P817 unexplained wealth from 2022 to 2025 are conservative or bare minimum, and that there are no double entries.

“These are all official documents. We meticulously reviewed them. Four eyes, six-yes review, and we used software technology in comparing records. We made sure that a remittance is not for two accounts. We made sure of that,” he said.
“In case of doubt or making an error, we don’t include it. Because if we have double entries, our estimate would exceed,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
articles.summary: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
articles.byline: Ed Walton and James Parrish for MetDesk

blocks.text: Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.

An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.

In Kosanica, Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.

Elsewhere in Europe, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.

Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.

Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.

blocks.caption: People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.

At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
