articles.title: UK politics live: Tories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign
articles.summary: Shadow minister says referendum was a ‘legitimate vote’ and PM is seeking to ‘reopen debate’ with statement on Russia’s involvement

blocks.text: Key events

items: 7m agoFarage says Reform UK would stop anyone being granted asylum for five years
14m agoEd Davey praises Burnham for confirming Russia tried to influence Brexit referendum result
32m agoTories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign

blocks.text: Farage says Reform UK would stop anyone being granted asylum for five years
Nigel Farage is set to announce a pledge to ban anyone from being granted asylum for five years if Reform were elected, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markThe Reform UK leader will announce a plan this morning to suspend the asylum system for a full parliamentary term and declare void any applications in progress. All asylum tribunals, legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes will be scrapped. A Reform government would not hear the around 90,000 outstanding asylum and humanitarian protection appeals and instead deport the claimants. The party would immediately close resettlement schemes that home secretary Shabana Mahmood recently said would reopen, with around a quarter of those admitted to the UK expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan. Reform says there is “no mandate” for such schemes and that anyone who has arrived under them would be deported. Any refugees granted asylum in the last five years would have their cases reviewed by the Home Office under the plans. Farage told The Telegraph: “The country is currently facing a national security emergency and the first duty of government is to protect its citizens. We cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose. A Reform government will always put British people first and protect our borders.” The party will also pledge to use tariffs to force countries to take back migrants.
Summing up his announcement on social media this morning, Farage said:
double quotation markToday, I am announcing that a Reform UK Government will SHUT DOWN the asylum system. This is a national security emergency and must be dealt with.
Ed Davey praises Burnham for confirming Russia tried to influence Brexit referendum result
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, has praised Andy Burnham for confirming that Russia tried to influence the outcome of the 2016 Brexit referendum. (See 9.28am.) In a statement, he said:

double quotation markI’m not going to agree with Andy Burnham on everything, but this statement needed to be said by a prime minister. After the Conservatives suppressed the truth for years, this took courage. We must do far more to protect our democracy from attack by the Kremlin and other hostile states, before it is too late.
Tories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign

Good morning. The last time Andy Burnham gave a statement to MPs after a recess, it went on for more than three hours. This prompted Kemi Badenoch to make a lewd joke later about the PM’s stamina (which she repeated at a party conference reception with an additional line about how she just had to “sit back and lie there”.) Today we are getting another post-recess, potentially wide-ranging statement from the PM, but the mood might not be so cordial.

Quite a lot has happened since MPs were last in the chamber almost a month ago, and they will want to ask the PM about issues like the cost of living, North Sea oil and gas, the Iran war and Ukraine. We have not been told yet exactly what Burnham’s statement will cover. But, as Aletha Adu reports, Burnham will talk about Brexit, restating what he told Labour’s conference about how he thinks it has done more harm than good and making the case for trying to find a better, closer relationship with the EU.
The statement will come after 3.30pm

Burnham has also given an interview to the Rest is Politics podcast and in it he confirmed that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum. This is one of those statements, quite common in politics, which are simultaneously unremarkable and newsworthy. Unremarkable – because it has been obvious to anyone reading the news for the past decade that the Russians were trying to help the leave campaign. And newsworthy – because it is not something that any previous PM has been keen to say.

For some years ministers have been using the line – set out in 2020 in the government’s response to the intelligence and security committee’s report on the threat posed by Russia – that “we have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU referendum”. That implies there is evidence of unsuccessful interference. But in the past prime ministers have not said that explicity. Post-2016 Tory PMs, whether they voted leave or remain, did not want to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the leave vote, and Keir Starmer was also reluctant to poke his stick into that particular hornets’ nest.

Burnham is taking a different approach. In his interview, Burnham was not asked, and did not say, if he thought that Russian interference had an impact on the result. Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, has been giving interview this morning and he told Times Radio:

double quotation markThe result is the result, and I think the prime minister has been very clear that he’s talking about attempts to interfere. The security minister has spoken about this before. I’m confident that both the British people and the British state are able to respond to and defend against these types of threats, but we need to be very honest that those threats exist.

(“I think the PM has been very clear” is the sort of thing a minister says when what they mean is “Of course, the PM wasn’t clear at all, but I’m happy to give you the line now.” Doughty later told LBC the Russians “haven’t succeeded in their many, many attempts to undermine our [democratic] processes”.)
The Conservatives have criticised Burnham for even raising the topic. Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, told Times Radio this morning:

double quotation markThat Brexit referendum was a legitimate vote. People voted in this country in record numbers to leave the European Union. And I actually think it’s very dangerous and divisive of the prime minister to reopen this debate in such an explosive fashion.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11am: Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, gives a speech.
11am: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesperson, hold a press conference.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Afternoon: MLAs (members of the legislative assembly) will vote on a no confidence motion in Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, over her support for a protest against the proposed Orange Order march down the Garvachy Road.
After 3.30pm: Andy Burnham makes a statement to MP.
Late afternoon: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, makes a statement to the Commons on the safety of MPs.

articles.title: Changing demographics in N.L. are driving demand for local lamb
articles.summary: Farmers and grocers say demand for lamb is on the rise in Newfoundland and Labrador.

image.caption: Farmers take their flock by boat from Tors Cove to Ship Island. (Dan Arsenault/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Farmers and grocers say demand for lamb is on the rise in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Farmers say the demand is ‘exciting,’ but conditions remain challenging
It’s a racket of crashing waves and bleating animals as sheep are loaded into a boat in Tors Cove, N.L.
Lambs and ewes are piled in for the voyage, as farmers work together for the animals' yearly vacation.
The sheep are being ferried to graze on nearby Ship Island. There, they’ll be safe from predators, and moving them will free up the farmers’ land to grow hay they’ll need badly this winter.
This is part of what it takes to raise sheep in Newfoundland, and farmers say lamb is a product customers can’t get enough of these days.
"We could all easily double our production and still not meet market challenges and or demands," sheep farmer David Hayes told CBC news.
N.L. farmers struggle to meet big demand for lamb
Hayes said part of that increase in demand is due to changing demographics in Newfoundland.
"Lamb is in very high demand now. Mostly a lot of new Canadians because it's a big part of their diet where it wasn't part of our traditional diet here," Hayes said.
David Hayes already has a waitlist of customers looking for lamb. (Dan Arsenault/CBC)
‘Way more tasty than the frozen’
Mohammed Kasmi is the owner of an international grocery, Andaluzia Market, in St. John’s. He loves to eat lamb. So do his customers.
"The quality of fresh local lamb is way more tasty than the frozen," Kasmi told CBC News.
But getting local lamb isn’t always possible to keep up with the demand he’s seeing.
Andaluzia market has been in business since 2020. Kasmi says he’s noticed an increase in demand in the last couple of years.

"International communities here like India, Afghanistan, Arabs, Middle East, I mean, everybody is interested in getting lamb in their menu, in their dishes. It's very highly recommended by the international communities," Kasmi said.
Owner of Andaluzia Market, Mohammed Kasmi, and butcher Youssef Aouachi say lamb sells out quick. (Madison Taylor/CBC)
Kasmi told CBC News he buys local lamb for his store whenever he can — whatever the price.

"We would like to support — all the time — the local farmers. We love to get from them the meat first. But unfortunately, if we don’t have any choice, we just have to look for different options," Kasmi said.
Alternatives to local include fresh meat from across Canada, and frozen from even further afield — all the way down under.
Kasmi’s freezers are stocked full of meat from New Zealand and Australia.
Morocco-born Kasmi said that back home, he used to eat lamb three or four times a week. But now, he substitutes beef in some of his dishes when lamb is hard to find.
He said his customers do the same, sometimes using goat as a replacement, too.
Sheep travel by boat to Ship Island, where they graze during the summer. (Dan Arsenault/CBC)
The future of the flock
On her farm in Port Kirwan, Brenda Aylward’s flock comes as soon as she calls.
Aylward is President of the Sheep Producers Association of Newfoundland and Labrador. She’s also noticed an increase in demand in their products.

"It's exciting to see the demand is there and that you are growing a product that people truly want and appreciate and value. It's also extremely frustrating because the growth potential is there, but being able to access the resources you need to grow quickly, it's not always an easy task," Aylward told CBC News.
Farmers in Newfoundland and Labrador say coyote predation is one of the challenges they face. (Katie Breen/CBC)
Aylward said major challenges farmers face are coyote predation, and access to adequate grazing pasture. But SPANL is working to address that.
Aylward said it's important for producers in the province to work together, and look to the future of the industry.
"It's a positive sign to see some of the younger producers and farmers’ kids," she said.

items: Meet your maker: Sheep to Sock Textile Festival highlights demand for wool
These N.L. sheep spend summer on their very own island

blocks.text: Aylward said that it’s important for producers to continue to make their voices heard to government entities for support.
The farmer encourages new people to get involved in the sheep industry.
"If we are supported fully by industry, by the public and by government ... it is going to become a very lucrative industry in years to come," Aylward said.
"I hope I'm still around to see that," she said.

articles.title: Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
articles.summary: Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize this weekend. Accepting the award, Sands criticized Germany's "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel.

image.caption: Accepting the award, lawyer and author Philippe Sands criticized Germany's 'inappropriate silence' regarding IsraelImage: Hannes P. Albert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair concluded on Sunday with the awarding of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade to the Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands.

Sands was honored in the presence of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
The jury said that his work was based on a "commitment to the universal rights of every human being, evidenced in his advocacy for victims of war crimes, racism, torture and colonial injustice."
Sands criticizes Germany's 'silence' on Israel

Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany for what he called its "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel and its actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
Sands said human rights abuses should be clearly named, especially among allies, stating: "It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth."
Philippe Sands: Peace through law

Sands, himself a descendent of Jews driven out of what is now Lviv in western Ukraine during the German occupation in the Second World War, became known to a broader audience through his 2016 book East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity.

The work, which details the lives of two Jewish lawyers, Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin, and the origins of international criminal law, was translated into dozens of languages, including German as Rückkehr nach Lemberg (Return to Lviv) in 2018.
"Germany knows all about ethnic cleansing," Sands said in Frankfurt, referring to criticism leveled at Israel by many states over its treatment of Palestinians.
"So why the silence? Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country."

Sands also condemned the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, as "appalling" and "a monstrous crime against the norms of international law" and acknowledged that Israel, like any state, has a right to defend itself.
"[But] this right is not unlimited and must be practiced within the boundaries of international law."

articles.title: How a loophole in Canada's species-at-risk law can leave wildlife in limbo
articles.summary: A new study finds a legal gap in Canada's Species at Risk Act can leave species waiting years for protection, with 153 of 288 cases overdue and still unresolved as of January 2025.

image.caption: A herd of caribou flee from a truck near Rivière-aux-Feuilles, Que. A new study found some caribou populations assessed as endangered have spent years awaiting federal listing decisions under the Species at Risk Act. (Rock Arssenault/Reuters)

blocks.text: A species can be assessed as endangered in Canada and still spend years waiting for Ottawa to decide whether to protect it — while the habitat it needs to survive keeps changing.

A new study found that of 288 species assessed as at risk since 2017, just 17 reached the Governor in Council — the federal cabinet body that makes the final listing decision — within the recommended timeline. Another 153 — more than half — were overdue and still waiting as of Jan. 25, 2025.

That includes populations of caribou, beluga whales and lake sturgeon that have been assessed as endangered or threatened while they wait for listing decisions that can trigger habitat protections and a recovery plan.

The researchers say the bottleneck falls in a gap in the Species at Risk Act (SARA). Ottawa has recommended timelines for moving assessments forward, but no statutory deadline for one crucial stage of the process.
The study doesn't say why the delays happen. Critics say the gap allows governments to put off tough choices between conservation and economic interests.

Peter Thompson, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at Simon Fraser University in Burnaby, B.C., and lead author of the study, said the government is routinely missing the timelines it set for itself.
"The government recommended one to two years, and they are consistently failing to meet that," he said.

A lake sturgeon rests along the riverbed. The Saskatchewan-Nelson River population was assessed as endangered in 2017 and has spent years awaiting a federal listing decision. (Eric Engbretson Underwater Photography/WWF-Canada)
The Saskatchewan-Nelson River population of lake sturgeon is one example. This ancient-looking fish can live for more than a century and grow up to three metres long.

COSEWIC, the independent scientific body that assesses wildlife, designated the population endangered in 2017 after declines of about 90 per cent since the 1960s. The study says it missed a recommended federal deadline for moving the assessment forward on Jan. 18, 2020, and was still awaiting the next step in the process five years later.
Thompson said the stakes are high because dams and other hydro projects have fragmented waterways and blocked the fish from moving between areas they rely on.
"It's preventing these species from going where they need to go to survive," he said.
What protection is delayed
A scientific assessment from COSEWIC does not, by itself, change a species' legal status under SARA. That depends on the federal government formally listing or reclassifying them.

Under the Species at Risk Act, listing an endangered or threatened species can trigger prohibitions against killing, harming, harassing, capturing or taking it. The law also requires a recovery strategy, which must identify critical habitat where possible. Once that habitat is identified, SARA contains provisions requiring its protection.

Those protections are especially important for aquatic species because SARA's core prohibitions apply to them across Canada, while for most terrestrial species they are generally limited to federal lands.

Drew Yewchuk, a lawyer and doctoral researcher at UBC's Peter A. Allard School of Law, says a gap in the Species at Risk Act can allow governments to postpone difficult decisions about protecting species. (Submitted by Drew Yewchuk)

Drew Yewchuk, a lawyer and doctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia's Peter A. Allard School of Law who did not work on the study, said habitat protection is one of SARA's most consequential tools.
"If the animals don't have habitat to live on, they don't live," he said.

SARA requires the environment minister to publish a response within 90 days of receiving a COSEWIC assessment. Once the Governor in Council receives that assessment, it has nine months to make a decision. But there is no explicit deadline for getting the assessment from the minister to the Governor in Council.
"It could just sit there forever because there's no timeline for the step," Yewchuk said.

Aquatic species stood out in the study. None of the 15 marine mammals or 49 marine fish assessed during the study period had been forwarded to the Governor in Council by the January 2025 cutoff. Ninety per cent of terrestrial mammals and 79 per cent of freshwater fish were still waiting.

Spawning sockeye salmon are seen making their way up the Adams River in Roderick Haig-Brown Provincial Park near Chase, B.C., in October 2011. Pacific salmon were among the aquatic species disproportionately affected by federal listing delays identified in the study. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)
More than biodiversity

Andrea Reid, a citizen of the Nisga'a Nation and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Fisheries Science at the University of British Columbia, said what is at stake goes beyond the loss of individual species.
"Because these fish are so deeply connected to who we are," Reid said. "It's not just food, it's all systems of tradition and culture and language."

The study identified 38 Pacific salmon populations delayed while the government continued collecting or analyzing information. Information collection was the most common explanation for delays examined by the researchers, followed by analysis. In 20 per cent of cases where the government provided an entry, no specific reason was given.

Andrea Reid, a citizen of the Nisga'a Nation and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Fisheries Science at the University of British Columbia, says Indigenous consultation should be built into the species-listing process rather than treated as a cause of delay. (Talon Gillis)
Indigenous consultation was also cited in some cases, but Reid cautioned against treating consultation itself as an obstacle.
"It certainly does take time. That is a reality, but that should be part of the planned process," she said.
Reid said listing is not always straightforward for Indigenous communities because restrictions can raise concerns about continued access to culturally important species.
"We need species to be adequately protected, but we also need cultural connection to be protected as well," she said.

A beluga whale swims in Hudson Bay outside Churchill, Man., in August 2022. Several beluga populations were among the marine mammals still awaiting a federal listing decision as of January 2025, years after their latest COSEWIC assessments. (Olivier Morin/AFP/Getty Images)
Few answers for long waits
Thompson said vague or absent explanations made it impossible for the researchers to determine why many individual species were delayed.
"It certainly seems like there is, at the very least, a lack of transparency in what is happening," he said.
Yewchuk went further, arguing that the gap allows governments to avoid publicly choosing between conservation and competing economic interests.
"It takes the pressure off of them to make hard calls about species conservation and allows them to just let the issue slide away," he said.

Environment and Climate Change Canada acknowledged the gap at the centre of the study. "SARA does not include a statutory timeline for the minister to provide a recommendation to the Governor in Council," the department said in a statement to CBC News.

It said 76 terrestrial species assessed since 2017 had missed the government's recommended timeline as of Jan. 25, 2025, and that some cases require more time for public, industry and Indigenous input.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada said aquatic listings can be more complex. "For aquatic species, listing can trigger protections across all waters where the species occurs, because these species are under federal jurisdiction," the department said in a statement. Since the study's January 2025 cutoff, the Governor in Council has received assessments for 15 aquatic species, starting the nine-month clock for listing decisions. On Friday, the government proposed adding or reclassifying all 15 under SARA.
Thompson said the broader problem is the pace of the process.
"We need to make the system more efficient and get these species the protections they need, or at least get a decision more quickly."

articles.title: Amid public anger over housing crisis, Spain's PM takes bold gamble to secure majority
articles.summary: By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Pedro Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities.

image.caption: People light their mobile phones during a minute of silence for María del Carmen Abascal, whose eviction sparked nationwide housing protests, during a demonstration demanding political action to alleviate Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Friday. (Albert Gea/Reuters)

blocks.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Oct. 5 amid unprecedented nationwide demonstrations over housing affordability.
The election, scheduled for Nov. 29, will bring Sánchez's parliamentary term to an end six months early, marking a bold political gamble by a prime minister known for taking risks.

The announcement followed the government's failure to secure parliamentary support for two proposed measures designed to address Spain's housing crisis. But a day after calling the election, the government approved the two decrees with some modifications. They include capping rents, a temporary ban on evictions and restricting companies from buying homes.

"It is only now, with protests and unrest spreading across Spain, that they have started paying attention to social housing and to the question of where people in this country can afford to live," said Sofía Olivares, 25, a student and spokesperson for housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo (Right to Housing).

While polls point to a right-wing victory, Sánchez is betting that the housing crisis will give him the political momentum needed to secure a parliamentary majority. Since becoming prime minister in 2018, he has had to rely on support from other parties to govern, as his socialist party has never held a majority in parliament.

items: Spanish PM calls snap election amid mounting housing crisis
Spanish pensioner Maricarmen, symbol of country's housing crisis, dead at 87

blocks.text: By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities. Chief among these are corruption investigations targeting his inner circle and the ongoing crisis in Ceuta.

This past summer, an influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco reached the Spanish enclave. While most have since returned, thousands remain on the streets or in makeshift camps, overwhelming local infrastructure and fuelling calls from the right for stricter migration controls.
Thousands of Moroccan migrants leave after storming Spanish enclave
Protests follow eviction, death of senior
The housing demonstrations erupted following the forced eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, who became a national symbol of the crisis before her death on Oct. 7.

In Madrid, protesters camped outside in scenes reminiscent of the Indignados, or 15-M, movement in 2011, an uprising that reshaped Spanish politics by breaking up the two-party monopoly and giving rise to smaller political parties.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, 87, waits for police to arrive before being evicted from her home in Madrid on Sept. 23. She died on Oct. 7. (Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)

In Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, part of the Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa and one of Spain's most popular tourist destinations, residents have also taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest over housing.

Olivares, of Derecho al Techo, blames the regional government for placing tourism above housing. "It constantly holds back housing policies to prioritize tourism," she said, arguing that limited land and a lack of rent controls have further worsened the crisis.

Over the past year, families across the Canary Islands — one of Spain's poorest regions, where almost 30 per cent of people are at risk of poverty — have faced dozens of evictions. This week alone, the housing group has supported more than nine families facing eviction.

Sofía Olivares, right, of the housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo is shown at a protest to stop the eviction of eight families, in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain, on Oct. 7. (Sonia Håkansson Rivero)
"Property funds buy the buildings they live in, refuse to renew their contracts and throw them out onto the street,” Olivares said, adding that promises to rehouse tenants are often broken.

The lack of public housing is another major concern. "We've also been about 10 years without any type of social housing being built in the Canary Islands," she said, adding that more than 30,000 people in the islands alone are on waiting lists for public housing.

Social housing accounts for about 1.7 per cent of Spain's housing stock, well below the level in most European Union countries. The Bank of Spain estimates that the country currently lacks about 750,000 homes, a deficit expected to exceed one million by 2028.

Demonstrators calling for a change in the tourism model in the Canary Islands gather in front of beachfront tourist accommodations in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria on May 18, 2025. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)
Right-wing parties expected to win: polls
Right-wing parties have argued that Sánchez's relatively open approach to migration is placing pressure on Spain’s housing market.

Unlike many European leaders, Sánchez has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. Earlier this year, his government also launched a sweeping regularization program aimed at integrating hundreds of thousands of undocumented workers into the formal economy.

Polling points to a conservative coalition led by the People’s Party, alongside the anti-immigration party Vox, as the most likely outcome of next month's election. Such a result would bring the far right into Spain's national government for the first time since the country's transition to democracy in 1975, following Francisco Franco's dictatorship.

items: 'Absolute chaos' as thousands of Moroccan migrants breach Spain's Ceuta border
Why Spain is aiming to regularize half a million undocumented migrants

blocks.text: The People's Party warns that the rent caps proposed by Sánchez will backfire by driving homes off the market. The government's measures also largely failed to win the support of the real estate industry, which says they don't address the root cause of the problem: Spain’s structural housing shortage.
"We are trying to address a supply crisis without sufficiently increasing supply," said María Matos, head of research and a spokesperson at Fotocasa, one of Spain's leading real estate platforms.
"By focusing on regulating properties, rental contracts and landlords, we risk making it even harder to bring homes on to the market."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is shown at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on Oct. 6. He has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. (Bernat Armangue/The Associated Press)

Fotocasa's latest data suggests landlords may already be responding to new housing measures. "In just eight days, long-term rental supply fell by 4.2 per cent,” Matos said. She warns that "measures designed to protect tenants can end up creating barriers for those still trying to find a home."

She also called for greater investment in public housing. "Since 2013, the development of new social housing has practically come to a standstill, forcing more households to compete in the private market."

Matos said she wants more land to be made available for development, alongside faster planning approvals. "We need to unlock public and private land, and speed up building permits to prevent projects from being delayed for years."
A man sleeps on a street near a protest calling for political action to address Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Oct. 6. (Nacho Doce/Reuters)

Garazi González, 36, who now lives with her partner and their baby in an apartment building belonging to his family, said she has experienced the affordability crisis first-hand and supports the protests "100 per cent."

Four years ago, after renting an apartment in central Madrid for eight years, she saw her monthly rent rise from 800 to 950 euros (about $1,275 to $1,500 Cdn). Her landlady then proposed raising it to 1,500 euros ($2,400 Cdn).
"She said prices in the area had gone up and she couldn't keep charging me so little. She gave me just one month to leave," González said.

items: Spain could impose a 100% tax on foreign home-buyers as tourism drives up housing costs

blocks.text: "I know people whose rents were raised to push them out, or who live in fear of being evicted from homes they've lived in for years. Others live in gentrified areas where vulture funds buy entire buildings and kick everyone out."
Despite her disappointment with the current government, González said preventing the far right from returning to power is now her biggest priority.

"I'm not entirely happy with the left because they haven't done enough on housing or other issues,” she said. "But I want to prevent fascism from coming back. I care about protecting social rights.... As a woman and a mother to a daughter, I worry deeply about her future."

articles.title: After being wiped off political map, what's next for the CAQ?
articles.summary: After securing dominant majority governments in back-to-back provincial elections, the Coalition Avenir Québec is now both without a seat in the National Assembly and without a leader, raising…

image.caption: Christine Fréchette stepped down as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec party last week after her party failed to win a single seat in the general election. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

After securing dominant majority governments in back-to-back provincial elections, the Coalition Avenir Québec is now both without a seat in the National Assembly and without a leader, raising questions about the party's future and viability as a political entity.
Party's executive director says lots of people interested in becoming next leader

After securing dominant majority governments in the 2018 and 2022 provincial elections, the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) is now both without a seat and without a leader, raising questions about the party's future and viability as a political entity.
Christine Fréchette resigned as party leader last Tuesday, the day after the election.

The CAQ, which was founded in 2011 with the goal of being a third alternative to sovereignty and federalism, was wiped off the political map, failing to pick up a single seat in the National Assembly despite receiving a little more than 572,000 votes.
The Parti Québécois, with 59 out of 127 seats, will form a minority government.
So what's next for the CAQ?
Here's a snapshot of where things stand as the party tries to pick up the pieces after a devastating election defeat.
Who is the next leader?
Following Fréchette's exit, the CAQ's next step is to appoint an interim leader.

In an interview with Radio-Canada's Tout un matin, the CAQ's executive director Brigitte Legault (not related to party co-founder and former premier François Legault) said the party's executive board will appoint someone on Oct. 17.
That person will be tasked, Legault says, with organizing the party's next leadership race. There is currently no timeline for that race.
Without naming names, Legault said there are many party members who are interested in becoming the next leader and taking on the task of reviving the CAQ.
"Many people are raising their hands left and right," she said.
"We have a challenge ahead of us. There are certain people who have been elected in the past, many of them actually, that want to roll up their sleeves."
Guillaume Rousseau, a lawyer and a CAQ candidate in this past election, told Radio-Canada he is keeping an open mind about running for the party leadership.
Rousseau finished fourth in Richmond, a riding in the Eastern Townships.

items: More on Guillaume Rousseau's ties to the CAQ, his work on secularism

blocks.text: Why the PQ’s victory is reviving calls for electoral reform in Quebec
Merger with another party?
The CAQ's colossal defeat raised questions about whether the party would simply cease to exist — or merge with another.
But Legault says that kind of talk is premature.
When asked if the party is considering a merger, specifically with the Conservative Party of Quebec, Legault said: "Not at all."
"We're a brand that has been in government for eight years and I think it's worth to try and relaunch everything."

items: CAQ fatigue key to sovereignist PQ's historic victory, fragile government

blocks.text: Ultimately, such decisions would be up to party members, she said, but added that based on what she's heard so far, a merger is not in the cards.

"They believe in this third path [between federalism and sovereignty], they believe in this balance that we struck between the economy and nationalism," Legault said. "We just need to re-inspire, recreate and find our creativity."
Ian Lafrenière, one of many longtime CAQ ministers who were defeated on election night, said the party needs to take a moment to reflect on how it can "reconnect with citizens."
"Thirteen per cent of people voted for us so there were lots of votes but no candidates were elected, so I think the option is still viable," Lafrenière said.
Brigitte Legault, seen here during a news conference in April of this year, says she's heard from former CAQ ministers and MNAs who are interested in leading the party. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)
Over half a million votes still count for something
If the CAQ does try to rebuild itself, their financial picture isn't clear but it appears it will have some financial backbone.

In Quebec electoral law, each authorized political party receives an annual allowance based on its share of the vote in the latest general election. The total pot to be divided between the parties is equivalent to $1.99 for each registered voter (6.4 million).
For the CAQ, that is an estimated $1.7 million annually — even if it has no one at the National Assembly.

items: Was Christine Fréchette forced off a political 'glass cliff'?

blocks.text: Quebec's Election Act also calls for parties who receive at least one per cent of the vote to get a reimbursement of 50 per cent of their campaign expenses. Candidates can also receive a reimbursement of 50 per cent of their individual campaign expenses if they were elected or received 15 per cent of the vote.
Legault says the CAQ failed to meet that 15-per-cent threshold in many ridings, but adds that the party also saved some money to prepare for the election's aftermath.
"We have employees, we have a party, we have members, we have activites to plan," Legault said. "We'll see with the new leader how we will proceed."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Antoni Nerestant has been with CBC Montreal since 2015. He's worked as a video journalist, a sports reporter and a web writer, covering everything from Quebec provincial politics to the 2022 Beijing Olympics.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Economic frustration helps fuel Alberta separatism — and these 4 charts suggest why
articles.summary: Alberta is a wealthy province. Yet economic frustration is part of what's driving the separation movement. But would independence improve Alberta's fortunes or bring new economic concerns?

image.caption: Retired petroleum engineer Morad Rizkalla says he plans to vote for the next step toward Alberta separation, hoping it will pressure Ottawa to address the province's economic grievances. (Ryan McLeod/CBC)

blocks.text: Alberta has long been seen as a province with an economic advantage — the wealthiest in Canada in terms of GDP per capita, rich in natural resources and no provincial sales tax.
But not all Albertans are feeling that prosperity.
Albertans frustrated with Ottawa point to a "lost decade" marred by unstable oil prices, cancelled pipeline projects and unemployment.
Morad Rizkalla, a retired petroleum engineer who spent nearly 40 years working in Alberta's energy sector, says cancelled pipelines have cost Alberta and Canada economic opportunities.
"We're like 20 years behind here," he said.
Years of economic frustration have helped fuel the province's separation debate, which is culminating in a vote this month to decide if Alberta should pursue independence.

"Over the past 10 years, the fact that Alberta has underperformed economically has probably given a bit more momentum ... to the movement and a bit more new support," said Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist with Alberta-based Servus Credit Union.
When oil prices crashed in 2014, investment in oil and natural gas projects plunged and the province fell into a recession in 2015 and 2016.

While the economy eventually recovered, the energy industry changed. Oil companies became more efficient and construction of major projects that once drove investment and job creation became harder to justify.
St-Arnaud says Albertans are still feeling the impact.
"We've seen the purchasing power of Albertans being lower. So it's 10 per cent lower now than it was in 2014," he said.
"That decline was sudden in 2015-2016, but then it has been stagnating since. So for the average Albertan, they're looking at their own situation and [thinking], well, I'm not getting ahead."

Alberta's unemployment rate has tracked above the national average since 2016, according to Statistics Canada, while average weekly earnings have struggled to keep pace with inflation over the same time.

Despite a decade of economic headwinds, there is plenty of optimism in Alberta's energy sector in 2026 as oil prices have reached $100 US per barrel again. A series of major projects are also in the works including the Pacific Link pipeline and LNG Canada Phase 2, in addition to record oilsands production.

The federal government has signalled support for Alberta's oil development by ending Canada's consumer carbon tax and the oilpatch emissions cap, but voters like Rizkalla haven't forgotten setbacks of the previous Liberal government.

"If something like the Northern Gateway and Energy East were built, they would have been just coming on now. Here we are in another oil boom and there would have been a huge impact on Canada — not just on Alberta, but on Canada and its GDP, unemployment all across the country."
Rizkalla says he plans to vote for the option on the Oct. 19 ballot that would direct Alberta to begin the process to hold a binding referendum on separation.
Rizkalla wants his vote to send a message to Ottawa to negotiate on issues such as equalization, Alberta's political representation in Parliament and access to markets.
But Rizkalla says he hasn't looked closely at the practicalities of separation — or the potential cost of forming a new nation, which some experts say could cost tens of billions.
What would separation actually change?
Some of the financial pressures facing Alberta would remain, regardless of its constitutional status.
Oil prices are determined by the rise and fall of global markets. Even with a return to skyhigh oil prices, companies have become more selective about investing billions of dollars into new projects.
In recent years, reinvestment in Alberta's oilsands has been a fraction of what it was before 2014.
Alberta would also still need to get its oil and natural gas to customers outside its borders.

"There's little doubt that Alberta has the economic ability to be on its own, in my opinion. But if you add in the uncertainty around Alberta being landlocked, that's a significant issue," said Martin Pelletier, senior portfolio manager at Calgary-based Trivest Wealth.
An independent Alberta would also have to determine pensions, currency, banking, taxation and trade.
Prominent voices for separation maintain Alberta would be better off economically on its own and say any outstanding issues could be resolved through negotiations with its neighbours.

"Our view is we can become independent, we can operate as an independent country and we can be successful financially," said Dennis Kalma, co-lead of independence organization Alberta Transition Council.
More like Brexit than Quebec?
Canada has been through separation debates before.
St-Arnaud lived in Montreal during the 1995 Quebec referendum and later in London during Britain's Brexit vote.

"In the case of Alberta, similar to Brexit, a lot of the reason for holding a referendum is more political than kind of social and cultural, as it was in Quebec. In Quebec, it was clear — let's create a French-speaking nation," he said.
Former British prime minister David Cameron, who called the 2016 Brexit referendum and campaigned against leaving the European Union, wouldn't necessarily draw the same comparison.

"Brexit was about whether we wanted to stay in a trade association with an element of political union. Canada is not a trade association with an element of political union. Canada is an amazing country with an incredible history," said Cameron while speaking at an energy conference in Calgary last month.

items: Brexit, 10 years later: What a regret-fuelled British town can teach Canada about referendums

blocks.text: Still, Brexit showed how complicated a breakup can be. "Leave" voters have since expressed regrets about rising food prices, border issues and political polarization.
"It's going to look like a divorce," said St-Arnaud. "It's going to be a long argument, a lot of lawyers involved and it's going to take a long time."

Former British Prime Minister David Cameron drew on his own referendum experience during a visit to Calgary on Sept. 28, saying there is never a guarantee what the results are going to be. (Josh McLean/CBC)
Independence supporters have pushed back on Brexit comparisons.
Lawyer Keith Wilson, who is also an advocate for separation with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide, says the situation is "fundamentally different."

"Brexit was about the U.K. moving away from its largest market, being Europe," he said in June. "Alberta independence is about Alberta moving closer to its largest market and the largest market in the world, the United States."
What could separation cost?
There have been varying estimates on the cost of Alberta separating.

Late last month, the Alberta Transition Council (ATC) released a budget and costing plan estimating one-time transition expenses of $5 billion, while predicting an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 to $32.1 billion each year.

items: Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence
Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report

blocks.text: A University of Calgary School of Public Policy report commissioned by the Alberta government predicts the cost of establishing a new country could range between $50 billion to $170 billion over a five-year period. The report found total provincial debt could skyrocket to between $324.1 billion to $442.3 billion.
Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta and a member of the report's advisory panel, says there's a lot of uncertainty.
"At the end of the day, it all affects our pockets," said Legge, who represents 130 business leaders in the province.
"I think that's a very financially challenging and risky gamble for all Albertans because nothing would be in our control."
But for now, he says the debate doesn't appear to be impacting business decisions.
"None of them have put anything on pause. None of them have said we're going to wait until we see what happens on Oct. 19."
Legge says that could change if Alberta moves toward independence.

articles.title: Germany news: Söder demands CDU supports of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt reveal themselves
articles.summary: Bavaria's conservative leader has called on bloc members who voted for an AfD parliamentary speaker to come forward. DW has more.

image.caption: Söder said the CDU members who voted for Tobias Rausch should show some "backbone" [File: September 2026]Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany news: Söder demands AfD supporters out themselves
Bavaria's conservative leader has called on bloc members who voted for an AfD parliamentary speaker to come forward. DW has more.

blocks.caption: Söder said the CDU members who voted for Tobias Rausch should show some "backbone" [File: September 2026]Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has accused some conservative bloc members in Saxony-Anhalt of being cowards
Bärbel Bas, Germany's education minister and the co-chair of the SPD, has resigned amid coalition infighting with Chancellor Merz's CDU

blocks.text: Here are the latest headlines and reports from across Germany on Monday, October 12:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
October 12, 2026
Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'
"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.

As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.
Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.
This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.
AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt

The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.

Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.
Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 3:36pm
MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla announced that the government has officially filed 39 court cases related to the massive flood control scandal.

During his first annual report delivered at the Office of the Ombudsman on Monday, October 12. Remulla said that 35 flood control cases have been filed in the Sandiganbayan, while 4 are being prosecuted in the Regional Trial Courts.
“Many more are under preliminary investigation and lifestyle checks,” Remulla said.
According to Remulla, these cases involve 52 individuals now facing charges. The high-profile list of respondents includes:

items: One sitting senator
One former senator
Four congressmen, including a former House Speaker
One former secretary and 33 employees of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)
Eight contractors and other private individuals

blocks.text: Addressing the public, Remulla explained that the filing of these 39 cases was the result of a rigorous, three-step process with "no shortcuts and no exemptions".

The anti-graft office first gathered evidence— including contracts, audit reports, and physical site inspections— before presenting the findings to the respondents to hear their side, and finally filing charges once the evidence was deemed airtight.
“Our cases are not decided by trending topics, hashtags, or the loudest comment section,” Remulla said.

The Ombudsman then urged the public not to be misled or used by paid online operations, advising the public to seek the truth not in comment sections, but by examining court documents, filed charges, and presented evidence.
“May mga taong nagbabayad para sa comments, para sa reactions, para sa mga fake accounts, para pagmukhaing boses ng taumbayan ang isang kasinungalingan,” Remulla said.
(There are people who pay for comments, for reactions, for fake accounts, just to make a lie look like the voice of the people.)
“Kaya sa ating mga kababayan: huwag tayong magpagamit,” he added.
(So to our fellow countrymen: let us not allow ourselves to be used.)

articles.title: How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
articles.summary: Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

image.caption: Electric buses, like this one in the Belgian capital of Brussels, are becoming increasingly common in European public transport systemsImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport has a negative impact on air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels that exceeded the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, which includes public but also private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gases emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated over a decade of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.
More electric buses, thanks to EU funds
The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — their vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.
EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.
Slow road to sustainability in some cities

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be at the end," Baierl said.
Another example are hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero-emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.
Many cities have not fully committed to zero-emissions despite EU targets
Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the ten largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero-emissions in buses or all public transport.
Rail transport is climate-friendly, but scarce

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.
"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."
Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.
Public transport's emissions go beyond the tailpipe

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."
But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.
Shifting from cars to a multimodal transport system
With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.
Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.
"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the model shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.
On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.
Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode".
Places with good public transport draw people in.
"Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," Baierl said.
Fact check: Eva Lopez
DW's data team contributed research to this project.
For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository. More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

This project is a collaboration among several media outlets in the European Data Journalism Network in context of Chat Europe. Project lead: DW. Contributing partners: Voxeurop, Denik Referendum, EUrologus, OBC Transeuropa.

articles.title: UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography
articles.summary: Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

image.caption: School uniforms are common in dozens of countries worldwideImage: Sven Simon/IMAGO

blocks.text: Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.
During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.
Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."
One in three schoolgirls reports harassment

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International. According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," says Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

blocks.caption: School uniforms are also iconic symbols of Japanese cultureImage: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: School uniforms often mandatory

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.
In the UK, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.
Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.
"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," says Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.
Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two MPs have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Diesel prices drop by P3/L; gasoline, kerosene rise over P1/L
articles.summary: Another round of mixed fuel price adjustments is set to take effect this week, with diesel prices set to roll back while gasoline and kerosene prices rise.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 3:16pm

Motorists line up at a gasoline station on March 1, 2026, two days before the scheduled fuel price hikes, as domestic pump prices are expected to rise amid escalating tensions between Iran and Israel, which have pushed up global oil and gasoline costs.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Another round of mixed fuel price adjustments is set to take effect this week, with diesel prices set to roll back while gasoline and kerosene prices rise.
The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following changes on Monday, October 12:

items: Diesel - down by P3.01 per liter
Gasoline - up by P1.56 per liter
Kerosene - up by P1.77 per liter

blocks.text: The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday morning, October 13, and will remain in effect until Monday next week, October 19.
Last week, an uneven fuel price movement was also implemented, with diesel prices dropping by P1.30 per liter, while gasoline rose by P1.93 per liter and kerosene by P3.30 per liter.
Price influence

The energy department explained that several factors affected this week’s price movements, including China’s export suspension, the availability of middle distillates, and recent global diesel supply relief measures.

The DOE said that while all oil products are affected by China’s recent announcement on the temporary suspension of refined petroleum product exports, recent international agreements have contributed to the rollback in diesel prices.
“Itong diesel kasi may malaking developments dito, positive developments,” DOE Oil Industry and Management Bureau Director Rino Abad said in a press briefing on Monday.
(“There are major, positive developments in diesel [supplies]”)

Among these developments aimed at easing the global diesel shortage, according to the DOE, was the agreement reached by G7 member countries at their meeting on October 2 to immediately release 100 million barrels of petroleum supplies, particularly diesel.
Another was the agreement between the United States and Russia to immediately release 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel to the US and global markets this October.

This will be followed by 3.75 million barrels in November, an additional 7.5 million barrels in the following months, and a potential additional 7.5 million barrels, depending on the capacity of refineries to process crude oil, according to the DOE.

Meanwhile, the upward price movement for kerosene has been attributed to its sensitivity to the availability and cost of middle distillates, a broader category of fuels that includes diesel and jet fuel.

“The G7 and US-Russia agreement could help ease the global diesel shortage, however, without the same emphasis on the release of additional supply for gasoline and kerosene, prices are expected to remain elevated for these products,” the DOE said.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ – Europe live
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv power plant among the facilities hit after US president claims ‘energy ceasefire’, while Kremlin yet to confirm any deal

blocks.text: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
We are restarting our live coverage of the latest developments in Europe after Donald Trump’s announcement of what he called an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Sunday evening that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian energy facilities despite the US president having claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant on Sunday, leading to power outages in the Ukrainian capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, adding: “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day”, referring to a type of Iranian-made drone commonly used in the conflict.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he was caught by surprise by Trump’s ceasefire announcement. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured, Ukrainian officials said. Two children were ‌among the injured, the regional governor said. In western ​Ukraine, ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people, officials ​said.

On Sunday morning Trump had announced that “effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, without further details.

Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me”, while Russia has still not confirmed its agreement. Zelenskyy said on Telegram yesterday that: “Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Reflecting a broad skepticism, the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said this morning that the bloc would welcome a truce but only “when it holds”. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
In other developments:

items: Nato Supreme Allied Cmdr Europe Alexus Grynkewich is due to deliver a warning to Russia at a security conference in Warsaw over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack from Moscow.
The Lithuanian ⁠foreign minister Kestutis ​Budrys said the EU should designate the Russian ‌intelligence agency GRU ​as ⁠a ​terrorist organisation.
The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Trump’s surprise ceasefire announcement came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel – temporarily lifting US sanactions – prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow.

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times has quoted officials in Europe as saying. They said the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 35m agoUkraine says Russia violated Trump's 'energy ceasefire'

blocks.text: We are expecting Volodymyr Zelenskyy to speak at the annual security conference in Warsaw alongside Polish prime minister Donald Tusk from 8.30am to 9.30am UK time this morning. Stay with us as we will bring you the key lines from what the two leaders say.

blocks.caption: Luke Harding

blocks.text: Luke Harding

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators. You can read the full story here:
